lines.text: You've probably heard it. The Bible was copied by hand for so long that nobody knows what it first said.
Like a game of telephone.
But telephone is one whisper passed down one line.
The Bible was copied in many places and many languages, and thousands of those copies still exist.
So we can lay them side by side and see exactly where they differ.
In 1947, shepherds found clay jars in a cave near the Dead Sea.
Inside was a scroll of Isaiah about a thousand years older than any Hebrew copy we had.
A thousand years of copying by hand. Small differences in spelling and wording. The same book.
Then there's the ground itself. For years, some scholars said King David was only a legend.
In 1993, archaeologists dug up a broken stone. Carved on it: the House of David.
None of this proves that God has spoken.
Evidence can show you the words are old and the history is real. It can't make you trust the one they're about.
The Bible makes its own claim, and it's a big one.
All Scripture is God-breathed.
So bring your hardest questions. This book has been answering them for a long time.
Then read it for yourself.
Two thousand years ago, the most powerful man on earth was called Caesar.
His face was on the coins. His armies were on the roads. And people called him lord.
Then a small group of people started saying three words. Jesus is Lord.
Today that sounds like something you'd hear in church. Back then it could get you killed.
Because if Jesus is Lord, Caesar isn't.
Jesus taught his followers to pray like this.
Your kingdom come, Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.
Look at what that prayer asks. It doesn't ask God to bless my side.
It asks for his kingdom to come. Which means mine has to make room.
Every nation is tempted to borrow God for its own story. Ours is too. So am I.
You can love your country. It's a good gift. But a good gift makes a terrible god.
Nations rise and nations fall. Rome did.
His kingdom is the one that can't be shaken.
we are receiving an unshakable kingdom
So here's the question. Whose kingdom are you praying for?
A king takes another man's wife. Then he has the man killed to cover it up.
The king's name is David. And for a while, nothing happens.
Then a prophet named Nathan walks in. He doesn't accuse the king. He tells him a story.
A rich man owns huge flocks. A poor man owns one little lamb, raised like a daughter.
A guest shows up. And the rich man takes the poor man's lamb for dinner.
David is furious. That man deserves to die, he says.
Nathan looks at him and says four words.
You are that man!
Here's why the story worked. David could see the sin clearly, as long as it belonged to somebody else.
So can we. We're experts on other people's faults and strangers to our own.
A king could have had Nathan killed. David says six words instead.
I have sinned against the LORD.
The way out of a blind spot starts when you let someone tell you the truth.
The Bible is sixty-six books, written by many authors over more than a thousand years.
And it tells one story.
It opens with God making a good world.
In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.
Then people decide they'd rather run it themselves. And everything cracks. With God, with each other, with the world itself.
God doesn't walk away. He chooses one family, Abraham's, and makes a promise.
All the families of the earth will be blessed through you.
The rest of the Old Testament follows that family. Rescued from slavery. Given a land. Ruled by kings. Carried into exile. And waiting.
Then the story does something no one saw coming. The author steps into it.
The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us.
Jesus lives the life we didn't. He dies the death we earned. And he walks out of the grave.
The last page sounds like the first.
Behold, I make all things new.
You're living between those two pages. Find your place in the story.
You've seen this one. On gym walls. On locker room doors.
I can do all things through Christ who gives me strength.
It sounds like a promise that you'll win.
So here's the first rule of reading the Bible. Read the verse next door.
Paul wrote this letter as a prisoner, in chains.
And one sentence earlier, he tells you what all things means.
Being filled and being hungry. Having plenty and having need.
to being filled and being hungry, to having plenty and having need
All things isn't winning. It's the full days and the hungry days. It's being all right when you lose.
That's a better promise than the one on the wall. It doesn't say you'll get what you want.
It says Christ will be enough when you don't.
So before you quote a verse, read the ones around it.
Mark is the shortest of the four Gospels, and the fastest. One word keeps showing up. Immediately.
There's no Christmas story. A grown man walks out of the wilderness and says the kingdom of God is near.
For eight chapters, everyone keeps asking the same thing. Who is this?
He calms a storm with a word. He heals the sick. He tells a man his sins are forgiven.
Then, right in the middle, Jesus turns the question around.
But what about you? Who do you say I am?
Peter answers. You are the Christ.
“But what about you?” Jesus asked. “Who do you say I am?” Peter answered, “You are the Christ.”
From that moment, the whole book walks toward a cross. Because this king came to do what no one expected.
For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many.
And at the cross, the one who finally says it out loud is a Roman soldier.
Truly this man was the Son of God!
Mark leaves you holding his question. Who do you say he is?
Did Jesus really rise from the dead? Start with the oldest report we have.
A little over twenty years after the cross, Paul writes a letter to the church in Corinth.
And in it he quotes something older. Something he says was handed on to him.
That Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that He appeared to Cephas and then to the Twelve.
Cephas is Peter. Many scholars think Paul received these words very early.
Then Paul adds something bold. More than five hundred people saw him at once, he says, and most of them are still alive.
In other words, go and ask them.
None of that forces anyone to believe. But it does rule out one idea. That the resurrection was a legend that grew slowly over centuries.
The claim was there at the start, from people who said they saw him.
So the real question isn't when the story began. It's whether they were telling the truth.
Some people think faith means never complaining to God. The Bible disagrees.
How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever? How long will You hide Your face from me?
That's a prayer. It's in the Bible's own prayer book, and it isn't alone. More psalms sound like this than any other kind.
They're called laments.
And they follow a path. Turn to God. Tell him what's wrong, plainly. Ask him to act. Then choose to trust him.
Watch David make that turn. Nothing around him has changed yet.
But I have trusted in Your loving devotion; my heart will rejoice in Your salvation.
Lament isn't the opposite of faith. It's what faith sounds like when it hurts.
You can bring him the whole truth. He already knows it.

films.title: The whole Bible in two minutes

lines.text: The Bible starts with God. He speaks, and there's a world.
He calls it good. And he makes people in his image, to look after it for him.
And God looked upon all that He had made, and indeed, it was very good.
Then the first people reach for the one thing God held back. And the damage spreads. Shame. Blame. A murder. A flood. A tower built to reach the sky.
God judges it. And he keeps showing mercy.
So God picks one man, Abraham, and makes him a promise. A people. A land. And a blessing meant for every family on earth.
all the families of the earth will be blessed through you.
Abraham's family grows into a nation, and the nation ends up as slaves in Egypt. God hears them. He spares them by the blood of a lamb and opens a road through the sea.
At Mount Sinai he makes a covenant with them, gives them his law, and has them build a tent so he can live among them.
I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.
God gives them the land. But they keep turning away, and each round is worse than the last.
They ask for a king. Saul fails. David loves God and fails badly too. And God promises David a son whose kingdom will never end.
your throne will be established forever.
The kingdom splits. The kings lead the people to idols, the prophets call them back, and they won't come. Babylon burns Jerusalem.
But in the dark, the prophets promise a new covenant and a coming king. Some of the exiles come home and rebuild. No son of David sits on the throne. The Old Testament ends looking ahead.
I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts.
Then God keeps his promises in person. Jesus says God's kingdom has come near. He heals, he forgives, and he speaks with an authority that belongs to God alone.
He dies on a Roman cross at Passover, carrying the sin of the world. And on the third day God raises him bodily from the dead.
that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures
Fifty days later the Spirit comes. The church starts in Jerusalem and spreads, Jews and Gentiles together, until the news about Jesus reaches Rome.
you will be My witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.
And the story ends where it began, with God and his people together. Only now the garden has become a city.
Jesus returns. Death is undone. And God makes his home with people forever.
Behold, I make all things new.
That's the whole Bible, from the garden to the city. And you're living somewhere on that road.
Before anything else, there's God. He speaks a world into being and calls it good. He makes people in his image to care for it.
The first people reach for what God held back, and the damage spreads. God judges. He also keeps showing mercy.
He calls one man, Abraham, and promises him a people, a land, and a blessing for every family on earth.
That family becomes a nation of slaves. God sets them free, opens a road through the sea, and gives them his law at Sinai.
He gives them the land, and they ask for a king. David loves God and still fails badly. God promises him a son whose kingdom will never end.
The kingdom falls. Babylon burns Jerusalem. But the prophets promise a new covenant and a coming king.
Then God keeps his promises in person. Jesus dies on a Roman cross, carrying the sin of the world. On the third day God raises him bodily from the dead.
The Spirit comes, and the church spreads to every nation. One day Jesus returns, death is undone, and God makes his home with people forever.
Behold, I make all things new.
One book. One story. Go read it.
The Bible isn't really one book. It's a library.
The Protestant Bible, the one most English readers hold, has sixty-six books. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include more in the Old Testament.
It comes in two parts. Thirty-nine books in the Old Testament and twenty-seven in the New, written in three languages: Hebrew, a little Aramaic, and Greek.
The books are shelved by kind. First come five books of law, Genesis through Deuteronomy. Then the history books, Joshua through Esther.
Next come poetry and wisdom, Job through the Song of Solomon. Then the prophets, the long books first and the twelve short ones after.
A Hebrew Bible holds the same books in a different order.
The New Testament opens with four Gospels. Each one is a portrait of Jesus: his life, his teaching, his death, and his resurrection.
Then Acts carries the story from Jerusalem to Rome.
After that come the letters, Romans through Jude. Thirteen name Paul as their writer. Hebrews doesn't name its author. Seven more follow.
Last stands Revelation, a book of visions.
These are different kinds of writing, and you read each kind differently. A poem isn't a law. A letter isn't a history. But together they tell one story.
The New Testament writers quote the Old on nearly every page, and they claim its story reaches its goal in Jesus of Nazareth.
And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, He explained to them what was written in all the Scriptures about Himself.
So before you read a page, ask what shelf it came from.
Genesis is the first book of the Bible. Its name means origin, or birth.
In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.
It tells how things began: the world, people, sin and death, the nations, and the people of Israel.
The book has two halves. Chapters one to eleven tell the story of the whole world. Chapters twelve to fifty narrow down to one family: Abraham, then Jacob, then Joseph.
One phrase works like a heading. This is the account of. It opens each of the book's ten sections.
This is the account of
Watch what chapter one says about people. In the ancient world, a king set up his image to show his rule. Genesis gives that dignity to every person, not only kings.
And the image isn't lost after the first sin.
So God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them.
Chapter three tells the first disobedience and what came of it. The damage spreads: a murder, a flood, a proud tower.
Everything that goes wrong in the Bible's story traces back here. So does the first hint of hope.
But the LORD God called out to the man, “Where are you?”
Christians differ on how literally to read chapters one to eleven. The book's own concern is who God is, who we are, and how God keeps his word.

Chapter twelve is the hinge the whole Bible turns on, from the world's story to Israel's. God calls Abram and promises him a great nation, a great name, and blessing for all the families of the earth.
all the families of the earth will be blessed through you.
The people of Genesis lie, scheme, play favorites, and betray each other. God works through all of it without excusing any of it.
Joseph says so to the brothers who sold him.
What you intended against me for evil, God intended for good.
Start with chapter one. The key chapters are one, three, nine, twelve, fifteen, twenty-two, thirty-two, and fifty.
And keep this in mind as you read. Describing an act isn't the same as approving it.
Genesis ends with the promise alive, but not yet kept. So keep reading.

films.title: Exodus: out of slavery, to God

lines.text: Exodus opens where Genesis ended. Jacob's family has become a nation, and the nation has become slaves.
The rescue doesn't begin with their faith. It begins with God's attention.
So God heard their groaning, and He remembered His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
The book has two halves. The first tells the rescue from Egypt and the road through the wilderness. The second takes place almost entirely at one mountain, Sinai.
Exodus gives as much space to where God will live as to how Israel got free.
The book turns on a name. At the bush, God tells Moses who he is.
I AM WHO I AM.
Pharaoh begins by asking who the LORD is, that he should obey him. The plagues are sent so that Egypt and Israel will know.
Israel keeps the first Passover and goes free, on a night of great sadness in Egypt. At the sea, God makes a way.
This is the Old Testament's defining act of salvation. The rest of the Bible keeps coming back to it.
The LORD is my strength and my song, and He has become my salvation.
Then comes the law, and the order matters. The laws aren't a ladder for earning God's favor. They're given to people he has already rescued.
In Hebrew, one word means both to serve as a slave and to serve God in worship. Exodus is a change of masters.
I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.
The last third of the book is about a tent. The golden calf nearly ends that hope. Moses pleads for the people, and God renews the covenant.
And the book ends at the goal the whole story has been moving toward.
The glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle.
Start with chapter one. The key chapters are three, twelve, fourteen, nineteen, twenty, thirty-two, thirty-four, and forty.
And don't hurry through the tabernacle chapters. Their length is part of the point.
God didn't only bring his people out. He came to live with them.

films.title: Leviticus: living near a holy God

lines.text: Leviticus begins where Exodus ends. The tent is built, and God's glory fills it, so that even Moses can't go in.
So here's the question. How can a holy God live among people who aren't holy, and the people live? This book is God's own answer.
I will walk among you and be your God, and you will be My people.
It has six parts. The offerings. The priests. Clean and unclean. The Day of Atonement, right at the center. Holiness in all of life. And vows.
The first half is about how to come near to God. The second is about how to live near him.
Be holy because I, the LORD your God, am holy.
The Hebrew word for an offering means something brought near. There were five kinds, from the burnt offering given whole to the peace offering shared at a family meal.
God himself gives the means of atonement. And the poor could bring two birds, or flour.
the priest will make atonement for him, and he will be forgiven.
Clean and unclean are about being fit to come near the holy place. Unclean doesn't mean sinful. A new mother or a mourner had done nothing wrong, and it ended with time and washing.
No one should use this book to call another person dirty.
You must distinguish between the holy and the common
Once a year the high priest, in plain linen, went behind the curtain into the Most Holy Place. And a goat carried the people's confessed sins away into the wilderness.
Jews still keep the day as Yom Kippur. Christians read it in the light of Jesus, as the book of Hebrews does.
because on this day atonement will be made for you to cleanse you

Then holiness leaves the tent for the field, the court, and the shop. Leave the edges of your field for the poor. Pay wages the same day. Judge fairly. Love the foreigner, because you were foreigners in Egypt.
And at the center of it all:
Love your neighbor as yourself. I am the LORD.
All Christians read Leviticus as God's word, and none of them offer its sacrifices, because Christ offered one sacrifice for sins for all time. They differ on how its laws apply now.
On any reading, nothing here gives anyone a reason for contempt toward any person.
Start with chapters sixteen and nineteen. Then the key chapters: one, ten, eleven, seventeen, twenty-five, and twenty-six.
Read it as the working rules of a sacred house.
It asks what it would mean for a whole life to belong to God.

films.title: Numbers: forty years in the wilderness

lines.text: Numbers carries Israel from Sinai to the edge of the promised land. And it tells why a trip of a few weeks took about forty years.
It's honest about what can happen after a rescue. And it's just as honest about God, who stays with people who keep failing.
They camped at the LORD’s command, and they set out at the LORD’s command
Two counts frame the book. First the generation that left Egypt, counted at Sinai. Then their children, counted on the plains of Moab.
In between come the march, the complaints, the refusal at Kadesh, Balaam, and Peor.
But I will bring your children
The camp is arranged around God. The tribes on four sides, the Levites nearest, and God's tent at the center.
Then comes one of the oldest blessings in the Bible. It's God's own gift. The priests only speak it.
May the LORD bless you and keep you.
Twelve scouts go into the land. All twelve agree it's good. Ten say it can't be taken.
The people hadn't miscounted the enemy. They had decided God couldn't be trusted. Moses pleads, God pardons, and still the refusal shapes the rest of their lives.
How long will they refuse to believe in Me
Balak of Moab hires a seer named Balaam to curse Israel. Four times he opens his mouth, and four times he can only bless.
His last oracle sees a star coming out of Jacob. Jewish readers before Jesus took it as a coming king, and Christians read it of Christ. Israel, down below, knows nothing about any of it.
A star will come forth from Jacob
The second count shows the promise outliving the people who refused it. Five daughters ask for their father's share, and God says they speak correctly.
The daughters of Zelophehad speak correctly.
The wars are hard pages, and Christians who receive this book as God's word read them in more than one way. On every reading, the commands were tied to one land and one time.
No one may use any page of this book as a reason for violence against anyone.
Start with chapters thirteen and fourteen. Then the key chapters: six, sixteen, twenty, twenty-one, twenty-four, and twenty-six.
Read the stories and the laws together, and watch Moses pray.
The book asks whether God can be trusted with what lies ahead.

films.title: Deuteronomy: love the LORD with all your heart

lines.text: Deuteronomy is almost all speech. Moses is at the end of his life, on the plains of Moab, preaching to the children of the generation that left Egypt.
He tells the story again, gives the law again, and pleads with them to hold on to God when he's gone.
These are the words that Moses spoke to all Israel

It has three addresses and a farewell. Moses looks back on the road. At the center he repeats the Ten Commandments and sets out the laws for the land. He renews the covenant. And he blesses the tribes.
One small word holds it all together. Today.
with all of us who are alive here today.
At the center stand two verses called the Shema. One God, loved with heart, soul, and strength.
And you shall love the LORD your God with all your heart.
Love here is a settled loyalty, shown in listening and obeying, and the words are meant to fill ordinary life. Jews have said them morning and evening for more than two thousand years.
God chose Israel not for its size or its goodness, but because he loved them.
Being chosen is a task. It's never a license to look down on anyone, and God loves the foreigner. So the great duty of the book is to remember.
But because the LORD loved you
The laws take the side of the powerless: the widow, the orphan, the foreigner, the debtor, the worker.
You are to pay his wages each day before sunset
The command about the peoples of Canaan is the hardest page, and Christians read it in more than one way. On every reading, it was tied to one land and one time.
No one may use these chapters to justify violence against any person or people.
The blessings and curses of chapter twenty-eight speak to a nation about a land. They're never God's verdict on one person's illness or loss.
Then comes the promise that God will change the heart itself, and the plea to choose life.
I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing.
And Moses sees the land he will not enter.
Start with chapters six and thirty. Then the key chapters: one, four, eight, twelve, eighteen, and thirty-four. Read it as preaching, out loud.
And keep the order straight. God's love comes first, and obedience answers it.
Joshua opens where Deuteronomy ends. Moses is dead, and Israel is camped east of the Jordan.
Joshua's name means the LORD saves. In Greek, it's the same word as the name Jesus.
cross over the Jordan into the land that I am giving to the children of Israel.
The book has four movements: entering, taking, dividing, and serving.
The long lists of towns and borders in the third part were title deeds. They say that God's promises land on the ground.
Not one of all the LORD’s good promises to the house of Israel had failed
Watch the crossing. When the priests carrying the ark step into the flooded Jordan, the river stops.
It's the Red Sea again, for a generation that never saw the first one. And twelve stones are set up so that children will ask.
so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the hand of the LORD is mighty
At Jericho and after, the book says whole cities were devoted to destruction at God's command, the young with the old.
Christians read this in more than one way, and none of them makes it easy. On every reading, it was tied to one land and one moment, and it was never renewed.
No one may use these chapters to justify violence against any person or people.
Watch who belongs. Rahab, a Canaanite, confesses Israel's God and is taken in with her family. Achan, an Israelite, steals from what was devoted to God and falls under the ban himself.
The line runs through faith, not birth.
the LORD your God is God in the heavens above and on the earth below.
In the end God gives rest on every side. At Shechem, old Joshua retells the whole story, from Abraham's family serving other gods to the gift of the land.
Only then comes the call.
Choose for yourselves this day whom you will serve.
The kindness comes first.
Start at chapter one. Then the key chapters: two, three, six, seven, twenty-one, and twenty-four. Read the whole book, not only the battles.
Don't skip the hard chapters. And don't read them alone.
Joshua is the story of a promise kept.
For the LORD your God is with you wherever you go.
Judges covers the years after Joshua and before the kings.
A generation grows up not knowing the LORD. And the book becomes an honest account of a people coming apart, and of a God who wouldn't give them up.
another generation rose up who did not know the LORD or the works that He had done for Israel.
An opening shows the land half taken and sets out a pattern. Then come the judges: from Othniel to Gideon, from Abimelech to Jephthah, and Samson.
The last five chapters have no judge at all. The beginning and the end answer each other.
Then the LORD raised up judges
Chapter two sets out a wheel. Israel serves other gods. Raiders come. The people cry out. And God raises up a judge. Then it starts again.
Mercy holds the wheel up, but it runs downhill. It's a spiral, not a circle.
for the LORD was moved to pity by their groaning
Look who God uses. A left-handed man. A woman. A farmer threshing in a winepress. The son of a prostitute. And a man who breaks nearly every vow.
The deliverance is God's, carried out through very human hands.
The Spirit of the LORD comes on Gideon, Jephthah, and Samson. But power isn't character. Gideon makes an object all Israel worships. Jephthah's rash vow costs his daughter.
Judges never treats God's gift as approval.
it became a snare to Gideon and his household.
The last chapters tell of a stolen idol, an outrage at Gibeah, and a civil war. The book presents them as the depths, never as a pattern.
In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes.
Readers weigh several of these stories in more than one way, and they differ on what that last line is asking for: a king, the LORD's own rule, or both.
On every reading, the book gives no nation, no church, and no person a warrant for violence against anyone.
Start with chapter two, slowly. Then the key chapters: four, six, nine, eleven, sixteen, and twenty-one.
Watch the refrains. Don't take the judges as models. And don't read the hard chapters alone.
Judges doesn't end with a solution. It ends with a need.

films.title: Ruth: loyal love in a hard time

lines.text: Ruth is set in the dark days of the judges, but it's told from inside one family in Bethlehem.
A famine drives them to Moab, and the men die there. Naomi turns for home with nothing. And her Moabite daughter-in-law won't leave her.
Your people will be my people, and your God will be my God.
The book has four chapters, and they balance. A scene on the road. A scene in the field. A scene at the threshing floor. A scene at the gate. The third is the turning point.
Naomi's emptiness in chapter one is answered by the child in her lap in chapter four.
I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty.
Watch for a Hebrew word, hesed. It names a love that keeps faith inside a relationship and goes beyond what duty requires.
Ruth shows it to Naomi. Boaz shows it in the field.
Nobody in Ruth sees a vision or a wonder. A famine ends. A harvest comes. Ruth happens to walk into the field of Boaz.
The storyteller lets you see God's hand in those ordinary turns without forcing the point.
under whose wings you have taken refuge.
A kinsman-redeemer was a near relative responsible for protecting a family's land, name, and people when they couldn't protect themselves.
Boaz takes on that role at cost to himself.
The man is a close relative. He is one of our kinsman-redeemers.
Then comes the surprise. Ruth is called the Moabitess again and again, yet she takes refuge in the LORD and becomes an ancestor of David.
He became the father of Jesse, the father of David.
The small family story turns out to be a hinge in Israel's history. And Matthew names Ruth in the family line of Jesus.
Read all four chapters in one sitting, slowly. Watch the words that keep coming back: return, empty and full, kindness, wings, redeem.
The book treats grief honestly, and it lets hope arrive slowly.
First Samuel carries Israel from the judges to the kings through three lives. Samuel, the answer to a childless woman's prayer. Saul, the first king. And David, anointed in secret.
It's a book about power: who holds it, and how it's given.
The LORD sends poverty and wealth; He humbles and He exalts.
It moves in seven stages. Samuel's birth and call. The ark lost and returned. Israel asks for a king. Saul's reign and rejection. David at Saul's court. David the fugitive. And the end of Saul.
The three lives overlap, and the handover is never clean.
Thus far the LORD has helped us.
The book begins when the word of the LORD was rare, and it becomes the story of a prophet through whom God speaks.
Speak, for Your servant is listening.
Kings stand or fall by whether they listen. Hearing and obeying count above sacrifice.
The elders ask for a king like all the nations. God calls it a rejection of his own rule, and then gives them one all the same.
Readers weigh why. The question the book asks is whether the king will rule as a servant under the word of God.
they have rejected Me as their king.
People keep judging by what they can see. Saul is a head taller than anyone. Samuel is taken with Jesse's tall eldest son. God looks somewhere else.
For man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart.
And David is chosen from the sheepfold.
Jonathan, Saul's heir, gives up his claim out of love for David and trust in God's choice. And twice David has Saul in his power and won't harm him.
It teaches restraint and trust in God's timing. It doesn't teach silence before injustice.
Jonathan loved him as himself.
The command against Amalek in chapter fifteen is read in more than one way, and none of them makes it easy.
On every reading, no people living today is Amalek, and no one may use this chapter to justify violence or contempt toward any person or people.
Start with Hannah's song in chapter two, slowly. Then the key chapters: three, four, eight, fifteen, sixteen, seventeen, and twenty-four.
Don't take its heroes as models in everything.
Then read Second Samuel. The promise to David is still ahead.

films.title: 2 Samuel: the king and the promise

lines.text: Second Samuel tells David's reign, from the day after Saul's death to his last years.
It gives the Bible both its highest picture of a king and its most honest one. A king God chose and loved, and a book that won't hide what he did with his power.
And they anointed him king over Israel.
It has five parts. King over Judah. The kingdom established, with Jerusalem, the ark, and the promise. David's sin and Nathan's rebuke. The troubles in David's house. And a closing collection.
Chapters eleven and twelve are the hinge.
The throne comes to David without his grasping for it. He mourns Saul and Jonathan, and each man who kills a rival to win his favor is rebuked.
When the ark comes to Jerusalem, David dances with all his might before the LORD.
danced with all his might before the LORD
David wants to build God a house. God turns the offer around. He will build David a house, a line of kings, with a throne established forever.
Your house and kingdom will endure forever before Me.
Jews before Christ read it of a son of David to come. Christians confess it kept in Jesus. The two part over how.
Then the hinge. David takes Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, and has Uriah killed. The text places the whole responsibility on David, and nothing in the story blames her.
Nathan, with nothing but a word from God, names the king's crime to his face. And David confesses.
I have sinned against the LORD.
He is forgiven.
But after it, the sword never leaves David's house. The rape of Tamar. A son murdered. Absalom's revolt. And a father weeping for the son who tried to take his throne.
The same king, the same God, and the same promise stand on both sides of chapter eleven.
O my son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom!
Start with chapter seven, slowly. Then chapters eleven and twelve, with Psalm fifty-one beside them.
The book gives no leader a shield against correction. Its own prophet named the king's sin.

films.title: Nehemiah: rebuilding the walls, and a people

lines.text: Nehemiah was a Jewish official at the Persian court. In 445 BC he came to Jerusalem and rebuilt its broken walls in fifty-two days.
Much of the book is his own account, full of quick prayers and strong feeling. He's a layman for whom prayer and planning are partners.
When I heard these words, I sat down and wept.
The book turns at chapter eight, from building the city to building the people.
First the burden and the night ride. Then the wall rebuilt against opposition. Then the law read and the covenant renewed, the wall dedicated, and the last reforms.
and they set their hands to this good work.
Chapter three names who built each section: priests, goldsmiths, perfumers, a ruler with his daughters. Then come mockery, threats, and plots.
Nehemiah's answer is the book in one sentence.
So we prayed to our God and posted a guard against them day and night.
In the middle of the work, poor families cry out. Famine, debt, and the king's tax have cost them their fields and even their children.
Nehemiah confronts the nobles, and they give back what they took. A rebuilt city with an unjust economy isn't a restored city.
What you are doing is not right.
The high point isn't the wall. It's the reading of the law. Ezra reads from daybreak until noon, the Levites explain it, and the people weep.
They're told to feast and share, because the joy of the LORD is their strength. Confession and a signed pledge follow.
explaining it and giving insight, so that the people could understand what was being read.
The ending has no triumph. Nehemiah comes back to find nearly every promise broken, and he acts, sometimes harshly. The text reports it without comment.
Nothing in it gives anyone today a warrant to strike or harm anyone. Walls can't make a people faithful by themselves.
Remember me, O my God, with favor.
Start with chapters one and two. Then the key chapters: five, eight, nine, and thirteen. Listen for Nehemiah's quick prayers, and don't skip the lists of names.
Promises made in a great assembly have to be kept in ordinary weeks.

films.title: Psalms: the prayer book of the Bible

lines.text: The Psalms are the prayer book of the Bible: a hundred and fifty poems.
Other parts of the Bible are God's word to his people. The Psalms are also his people's words to him, which he has taken into Scripture.
Trust in Him at all times, O people; pour out your hearts before Him.
They aren't one long list. Two gateway psalms open the collection. Five books follow. And five psalms of Hallelujah close it.
Each of the first four books ends with a short blessing of God.
Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting. Amen and Amen.
The largest group of psalms are laments. They complain to God about enemies, about guilt, and about God's own apparent absence, and they do it inside the covenant.
How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever?
Most turn toward trust. A few, like Psalm eighty-eight, never do. Protest can be a form of faith.
Praise in the Psalms is a response. To God's work in creation. To his rescue of Israel. To his help in one crisis.
One person's rescue becomes the whole community's reason to worship.
Let everything that has breath praise the LORD!
Under every lament and every hymn lies one conviction: the LORD reigns.
Book Three ends by asking how God's covenant with David can stand when the crown lies in the dust. Book Four answers by proclaiming that the LORD is king.
The LORD reigns! He is robed in majesty
The Gospels show Jesus praying the psalms in his suffering. From the cross he cries the opening of Psalm twenty-two.
My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?
Christians since the early church have prayed the Psalms both as their own prayers and as the prayers of Christ.
Start at the gateway, with Psalm one. The key psalms are one, two, twenty-two, twenty-three, fifty-one, seventy-three, eighty-nine, and a hundred and ten.
Read each one whole, slowly, and out loud.
Wisdom in Proverbs isn't cleverness or book learning. It's skill in living: the ability to see how God's world works and to act in step with it.
Its motto comes in the first chapter.
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge.
Proverbs is a collection of collections. Nine chapters of longer poems. The proverbs of Solomon. The words of the wise. A second collection copied by Hezekiah's men. And the words of Agur and Lemuel.
The book pictures life as a road with two paths. Choices that look small, a companion, a loan, a glance, a lie, set a person on one road or the other.
Proverbs trains you to see where a path ends before you step onto it.
The path of the righteous is like the first gleam of dawn
In chapters one, eight, and nine, wisdom speaks as a woman who calls out in public places, and who was there with God when he made the world. Her rival, Folly, calls too.
So choosing wisdom means accepting an invitation, not only mastering a set of rules.
Wisdom calls out in the street, she lifts her voice in the square
Few subjects get more attention in Proverbs than the tongue. Honest lips and lying lips. Gossip and discretion. Flattery and faithful rebuke.
A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.
Restraint in speech is treated again and again as a mark of wisdom.
Proverbs praises diligence and warns the sluggard. But it also warns against trusting riches and against oppressing the poor.
Wealth is a real good in this book, but always a lesser one than wisdom, righteousness, and a good name.
Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD
Read Proverbs as proverbs. A proverb is a compressed observation about how life usually goes under God. It isn't a guarantee for every case.
Start with chapter one. The key chapters are one, three, eight, nine, ten, twenty-two, and thirty-one.
It's skill for ordinary days, and it begins here.
Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and lean not on your own understanding.

films.title: Isaiah: the Holy One who comforts

lines.text: Isaiah spoke to the kings of Judah in the days of the Assyrian empire. His signature name for God comes from a vision: the Holy One of Israel.
Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Hosts; all the earth is full of His glory.
Holiness exposes human pride. It also means God's commitment to his people.
The book has three major parts. The first speaks to Judah in the prophet's own day: judgment, threaded with promise.
From chapter forty, the voice speaks comfort to a people in exile. And the last chapters speak to a community back in the land, still waiting.
“Comfort, comfort My people,” says your God.
Again and again the kings of Judah have to choose between trusting God and trusting military power or foreign alliances. Ahaz chooses Assyria. Hezekiah prays.
The book's verdict is that faith is the only real security.
If you do not stand firm in your faith, then you will not stand at all.
God's judgment in Isaiah is real and severe, and it falls on Judah and on every nation alike. But it isn't where the book ends.
Through it God preserves a remnant, a people who will return to him.
Though your sins are like scarlet, they will be as white as snow
Isaiah gives three portraits of the one through whom God will act. A royal child from David's line. A Servant who suffers for others. And an anointed messenger of good news.
But He was pierced for our transgressions.
Jewish interpreters have often read the Servant as Israel. The New Testament sees all three in Jesus.
Isaiah sees Zion becoming the place where all nations come to learn God's ways. Israel's calling turns out to be for the sake of the whole world.
And the last chapters reach beyond Israel's history to new heavens and a new earth.
For behold, I will create new heavens and a new earth.
Isaiah is mostly poetry. Keep three horizons in view: the prophet's own day, the exile and return, and the far future.
The key chapters are one, six, seven, nine, thirty-seven, forty, fifty-three, and sixty-five.
Empires in this book come and go. One thing doesn't.
The word of our God stands forever.

Jeremiah lived through the end of the world as his people knew it. He was called as a young man, and he spoke for about forty years while Judah slid from reform into denial, and from denial into ruin.
Then everything he had said came true.
Before I formed you in the womb I knew you
It isn't a tidy life story. Poems of judgment, sermons, stories of arrests, acted signs, letters, and raw private prayers are gathered in seven parts.
And at its heart, in chapters thirty to thirty-three, stands a small book of comfort.
to build and plant.
Jeremiah attacks what Judah trusted instead of God. The temple as a charm. Prophets who promised peace. Ritual without obedience.
He calls the temple a den of robbers, words Jesus later used. The forms of faith can become a hiding place from God.
Do not trust in deceptive words
No other prophet lets you hear so much of his own pain. Jeremiah accuses God of deceiving him and curses the day he was born. Yet he can't hold the word in.
His message becomes a fire burning in my heart, shut up in my bones.
Faithfulness can include lament and protest brought straight to God.
He writes to the exiles: build houses, seek the welfare of Babylon, and wait.
The famous promise of a future and a hope was spoken to people facing seventy years of exile. It's a promise through suffering, not a guarantee of success.
to give you a future and a hope.
In chapter thirty-one, God promises a new covenant: his law written on the heart, and sin forgiven.
I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts.
The New Testament claims it as fulfilled, from the cup Jesus calls the new covenant to the letter to the Hebrews.
Start at chapter one. Then the key chapters: seven, twenty, twenty-nine, thirty-one, thirty-six, and fifty-two.
And remember that its call to surrender to Babylon was a word for one moment, not a rule about politics.
Judgment is not God's last word.
Daniel is two books in one. Chapters one to six are stories of Daniel and three friends, taken from Judah to serve the king of Babylon.
Chapters seven to twelve are visions of empires, and of the kingdom of God that outlasts them all.
To these four young men God gave knowledge and understanding
Chapter one is in Hebrew. Chapters two to seven are in Aramaic, framed by two visions of four kingdoms followed by God's kingdom.
Then the book returns to Hebrew: the ram and the goat, a prayer, and a final vision.
the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed
Every chapter presses one claim. God gives kingdoms and takes them away. Proud kings are made to confess it.
The Most High rules over the kingdom of mankind.
Empires are real and dangerous. But they're temporary, and they answer to a higher throne.
Daniel and his friends learn Babylon's language and serve its kings with integrity. But they draw the line at worship.
Three of them won't bow to the golden statue. They trust God to save them, and they trust him even if he doesn't.
But even if He does not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods.
When a decree forbids prayer, Daniel keeps praying at his open window, just as he had done before.
He's put into the lions' den and brought out alive. And a foreign king confesses that God's kingdom will not be destroyed.
My God sent His angel and shut the mouths of the lions.
In the visions, empires rise like beasts from the sea. And one like a son of man is given a kingdom that will not pass away.
Jesus took that title for himself.
I saw One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven.
Many read the four kingdoms as Babylon, Media-Persia, Greece, and Rome. Many others read them as Babylon, Media, Persia, and Greece. Careful readers also differ on when the book was finished.
The visions are pictures, not a code for the news. The book's own concern is endurance and hope.
Start with chapter one. The key chapters are two, three, four, six, seven, nine, and twelve.
Empires rise and empires pass. The Most High rules.

films.title: Amos: let justice roll on like a river

lines.text: Around 760 BC, a herdsman from Tekoa in Judah went north to Israel, which was then at its greatest wealth in generations.
The shrines were crowded, and the rich had houses decorated with ivory. Amos looked beneath the prosperity.
But the LORD took me from following the flock
The book has three parts. A ring of judgments on the nations, which closes on Judah and then on Israel. Sermons, laments, and woes. And five visions, ending in a promise of restoration.
The LORD roars from Zion and raises His voice from Jerusalem
It opens with a trap. God judges Israel's neighbors for cruelty every people knows is wrong, and a first hearer would have agreed with every word.
Then the trap closes on Judah, and at greatest length on Israel, who sell the needy for a pair of sandals.
they sell the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals.
God refuses Israel's feasts and songs in some of the hardest words in the Bible.
But let justice roll on like a river, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream.
Amos doesn't reject worship as such. He attacks worship cut off from obedience, and comfort that doesn't grieve.
In the visions, Amos pleads twice and God relents. Then a plumb line shows Israel out of true.
Amaziah, the priest of the king's shrine, tells him to go home. Amos answers that the LORD took him from following the flock.
I am setting a plumb line among My people Israel
The book ends in hope. God will restore the fallen tent of David and plant his people in their land.
James quoted these words in Jerusalem, about the Gentiles coming to faith. They make no claim about any modern state or border.
In that day I will restore the fallen tent of David.
Readers across the political spectrum have claimed Amos. The book itself speaks to God's people and their leaders, and its standard is God's covenant, not any modern program or party.
Start with chapter five. Then the key chapters: one, two, three, seven, and nine.
Read the charges for what they name, and let them land on yourself before anyone else.
And hear the invitation inside the warning.
Seek Me and live!

films.title: Jonah: the prophet who ran from mercy

lines.text: Jonah is unlike the other prophets. It's almost all story, with one short sentence of prophecy.
God sends Jonah to Nineveh, a great city of Assyria, Israel's enemy. Jonah boards a ship for Tarshish, at the far end of the known world.
Jonah, however, got up to flee to Tarshish, away from the presence of the LORD.
It has four chapters. Jonah runs, and the sailors fear the LORD. His prayer from the depths. Nineveh turns. Then Jonah's anger, and God's question.
The last chapter is the real climax, and the book ends on a question Jonah never answers.
Jonah confesses the LORD as the God who made the sea and the dry land, and the book shows it. God appoints a storm, a fish, a plant, a worm, and an east wind.
Everything in the book obeys God except his prophet.
Now the LORD had appointed a great fish to swallow Jonah
Jonah goes down to the port, down into the ship, down to the roots of the mountains. From the fish he prays a psalm of thanks, and God brings him up.
But You raised my life from the pit, O LORD my God!
Jesus took this as the sign of Jonah, a picture of his own death, burial, and resurrection.
The sailors, a king, and a whole city respond to God more readily than his prophet does. Jonah's warning offers no mercy, yet Nineveh turns, and God relents.
His warnings of judgment are meant to lead people to turn.
He relented from the disaster He had threatened to bring upon them.
Jonah is furious, and he explains why he ran.
I knew that You are a gracious and compassionate God, slow to anger.
God gives him a plant, then takes it away, and ends the book with a question.
Many readers, Jewish and Christian, take Jonah as history. Many others read it as a teaching story. Some hold both.
Whatever a reader decides, the book's message is the same.
Start with chapter one and read all four. Watch three words: great, down, and appointed.
The worst misreading argues about the fish and misses the question about mercy.
So should I not care about the great city of Nineveh
Jonah never answers that question. It's asked of the reader too.
Matthew tells the story of Jesus with Israel's Scriptures always in view. It opens with a genealogy that traces him through King David to Abraham.
Its Jesus is the promised Messiah, the teacher greater than Moses, and Immanuel, which means God with us.
they will call Him Immanuel” (which means, “God with us”).
Matthew alternates story and speech. Five long discourses, beginning with the Sermon on the Mount, each close with the same formula.
They make this the fullest collection of Jesus' words among the Gospels.
When Jesus had finished saying these things
Matthew sees Jesus as the goal of Israel's Scriptures. The fulfillment formulas, the genealogy, and the patterns that echo Moses and the exodus present his story as the completion of Israel's story.
I have not come to abolish them, but to fulfill them.
The kingdom of heaven means God's reign, arriving in Jesus' own person and work.
It's present in his healings and teaching. It's hidden and growing, like a mustard seed. And it's still to come in fullness.
Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near.
In the middle of the book, Peter confesses who Jesus is.
You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.
From that time, Jesus begins to show his disciples that he must suffer, be killed, and on the third day be raised. The story turns toward Jerusalem and the cross.
Matthew is a deeply Jewish book. Its sharp words against scribes and Pharisees belong to an argument among Jews about Israel's Scriptures. They are no verdict on the Jewish people.
Jesus is sent first to Israel, and the Gospel ends with all nations.
Therefore go and make disciples of all nations
Start with chapter one. The key chapters are one, five, six, thirteen, sixteen, twenty-six, and twenty-eight.
The Gospel opens with the name Immanuel, and it closes with the risen Jesus keeping it.
And surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age.

films.title: Mark: the story at a run

lines.text: Mark is the shortest of the four Gospels, and it moves at speed. There's no birth story and no long sermon. The word translated immediately appears more than forty times.
Its first line works as a title.
This is the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God.
The first half is set in Galilee, full of authority and questions. Its hinge is Peter's confession.
From there the story walks the road to Jerusalem, tells the passion by the hour, and ends at an empty tomb.
The question of who Jesus is runs through the whole book. You know the answer from the first line.
The drama is in watching the characters struggle toward it, often getting the words right and the meaning wrong.
Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?
On the road to Jerusalem, Jesus predicts his death and resurrection three times. And each time he teaches what following him means: deny yourself, and be the servant of all.
For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many.
Mark doesn't flatter the disciples. They misunderstand. They fall asleep in Gethsemane. They flee. And Peter denies Jesus three times.
Yet the message at the tomb names Peter in particular.
But go, tell His disciples and Peter
The first human being in Mark to call Jesus the Son of God is a Roman centurion at the foot of the cross, at the moment of his death.
Truly this man was the Son of God!
The Son of God is recognized fully only at the cross.
Read Mark in one sitting if you can. Its force comes from its pace. The key chapters are one, four, eight, ten, thirteen, fifteen, and sixteen.
The oldest complete copies end with the women at the tomb.
Mark holds authority and suffering together.

films.title: Luke: good news for the lost

lines.text: Luke opens with a formal preface. Many have written accounts. The material was handed down by eyewitnesses. And he has investigated everything carefully.
It's the first of two books by the same author, and it presents Jesus as Savior.
Today in the city of David a Savior has been born to you.
After the births of John and Jesus comes the ministry in Galilee. Then the turning point is marked in the text, and the long central section is framed as the road to Jerusalem.
The book ends where it began, in the temple.
Jesus resolutely set out for Jerusalem.
Luke gives more attention to wealth and poverty than any other Gospel, and women are prominent throughout. Samaritans, tax collectors, and sinners are welcomed.
In his first sermon, Jesus reads from Isaiah and says it's fulfilled that day.
He has anointed Me to preach good news to the poor.
The parables of the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the lost son show God's joy in finding the lost. They also expose the resentment of those who think they were never lost.
Jesus sums up the whole book in one line.
For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.
Luke shows Jesus praying at the turning points of his life: at his baptism, before choosing the Twelve, at the transfiguration, in Gethsemane, and on the cross.
Prayer in Luke is the ordinary posture of those who wait on God.
Lord, teach us to pray
The word today carries weight in Luke. Salvation is present, not only future, and it brings joy.
On the Emmaus road, the risen Jesus opens the Scriptures to two disciples who had been hoping, and had given up.
Were not our hearts burning within us as He spoke with us on the road
Start with chapter one. The key chapters are one, two, four, fifteen, nineteen, and twenty-four. Watch the meals, the prayers, and the word today.
And read on. The same author's second book is Acts.
John is the fourth of the four Gospels. It tells the same story as Matthew, Mark, and Luke from a different height.
It begins before the world was made. And soon comes the sentence the whole book hangs on.
The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us.
John is built with care. An opening poem. A first half built around signs. And a second half that slows almost to a stop: five chapters are given to one evening.
Then come the cross, the resurrection, and a closing scene by the lake.
Jesus knew that His hour had come
John calls Jesus' miracles signs, because each one points beyond itself to who he is. The first half is built around seven of them.
Signs can start faith. But faith that only wants miracles is thin.
Jesus performed this, the first of His signs, at Cana in Galilee.
Seven times Jesus says I am, and adds a picture. Bread. Light. A gate. A shepherd. Resurrection and life. The way. The true vine.
I am the bread of life.
Each one takes something people can't live without and says: this is what I am for you.
The verb believe comes ninety-eight times in John, and the noun faith never does. Believing is something you do: coming to Jesus, trusting him, staying with him.
And eternal life, in John, is life with God that begins now.
to those who believed in His name, He gave the right to become children of God
The second half opens when Jesus knows his hour has come. He washes his disciples' feet and gives them a new command.
A new commandment I give you: Love one another.
In John, the glory of God is seen most clearly at the cross. Then come the empty tomb and the risen Jesus.
Start at chapter one and read slowly. The key chapters are one, three, six, eleven, thirteen, seventeen, and twenty.
One caution. When John speaks of the Jews, he usually means the Jerusalem authorities. Jesus and nearly everyone in the story are Jews.
John tells you plainly why he wrote.
These are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God.

films.title: Acts: to the ends of the earth

lines.text: Acts picks up where the Gospel of Luke leaves off. Luke's first book was about all that Jesus began to do and to teach. That suggests Acts is about what Jesus continues to do, through his Spirit and his people.
You will be My witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.
Acts moves outward from Jerusalem. First the city. Then Judea and Samaria. Then the door to the nations.
The second half belongs largely to Paul, and it ends with him in Rome under guard, still teaching.
Boldly and freely he proclaimed the kingdom of God
The Spirit is the driving force of Acts. He comes at Pentecost, fills believers for bold speech, guides decisions, and sets apart messengers.
I will pour out My Spirit on all people.
And he falls on Samaritans and Gentiles in ways that force the church to recognize them as full members.
The key word of the book is witness. Stephen's witness costs him his life.
Lord, do not hold this sin against them.
Almost every advance in Acts comes through opposition, and Luke presents none of it as defeat. Persecution scatters the church, and so spreads the word.
Acts traces the good news across line after line: Samaritans, an official from Ethiopia, a Roman centurion. Each crossing is contested.
The council in Jerusalem settles the central question. Gentiles are saved by grace, as Jews are.
I now truly understand that God does not show favoritism
Saul, the church's fiercest opponent, meets the risen Jesus and becomes its messenger.
Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?
Acts insists that faith in Jesus fulfills Israel's hope and does not replace it. The first believers are Jews, and Paul on trial says he stands accused because of the hope of Israel.

All Christians confess that the Holy Spirit is given to the church. They differ on how much of the pattern in Acts is meant for every church: the order of faith, baptism, and receiving the Spirit, and whether speaking in tongues is a regular sign of the Spirit's coming.
This film takes no side.
Start with chapter one, and read for the large movement, from Jerusalem outward. Not every event in Acts is a rule for every church.
The key chapters are one, two, seven, nine, ten, fifteen, seventeen, and twenty-eight.
I wrote about all that Jesus began to do and to teach
Acts ends in Rome, with Paul under guard and still teaching.

films.title: Romans: the good news, set out

lines.text: Romans is a letter, the longest Paul wrote. He sent it to the Christians in Rome, Jewish and Gentile believers he had not yet met, to introduce himself and the gospel he preached. He states his theme early.
I am not ashamed of the gospel, because it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes.
Romans moves in large blocks. What is wrong with the whole human race. What God has done about it. The new life that follows. God and Israel. And the life of a people shaped by mercy.
The first great turn is two words: but now.
But now, apart from the law, the righteousness of God has been revealed
Paul first shows that the whole human race, Gentile and Jew, stands guilty before God.
For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.
Romans treats sin as more than wrong acts. It's a power that reigns. So people need more than self-improvement. They need to be rescued.
God sets people right with himself freely, by grace, through Jesus' death, and they receive it by faith.
Faith means trust. It isn't a good deed that earns a reward.
justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.
Grace doesn't mean going on in sin. Believers have died with Christ and live a new life.
There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
The Spirit gives life, makes them God's children, and holds them in a love nothing can break.
Chapters nine to eleven are not a detour. Paul asks whether God has kept his promises to Israel, and he answers that God's word has not failed.
Then he tells a church of Jewish and Gentile believers to welcome one another.
Accept one another, then, just as Christ accepted you

All Christians confess that God sets people right with himself by grace, through Christ. They read some of Paul's phrases in more than one way: what he means by works of the law, and whether one phrase means faith in Christ or the faithfulness of Christ.
This film takes no side.
Start with chapter one, and read it aloud, in large sections. Many famous verses mean more inside their paragraph than on a poster.
The key chapters are one, three, four, five, six, eight, nine, and twelve.
To all in Rome who are loved by God and called to be saints: Grace and peace to you
Romans is the good news, set out for people Paul had not yet met.

films.title: 1 Corinthians: a gifted church, coming apart

lines.text: First Corinthians is a real letter to a real church with real trouble. The church in Corinth was young, rich in gifts and eloquent speech, and coming apart.
Paul neither gives up on it nor flatters it.
To the church of God in Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus and called to be holy
Chapters one to six answer what Paul has heard by report. Chapters seven to sixteen answer the questions the Corinthians wrote to him, many marked by the words now about.
The letter begins with the cross and ends with the resurrection.
Now for the matters you wrote about
Corinth prized eloquence, knowledge, and status. Paul answers with a crucified Messiah, which looked like foolishness.
For I resolved to know nothing while I was with you except Jesus Christ and Him crucified.
The cross doesn't only save. It reorders what counts as strength and wisdom.
The Spirit gives varied gifts to one body for the common good. Division is not a matter of taste. It's an attack on what God is building.
Now you are the body of Christ, and each of you is a member of it.
Unity is not sameness, and the weaker members are indispensable.
Chapter thirteen is often read at weddings. In its setting it's a rebuke to a church competing over spiritual gifts.
Love is patient, love is kind.
Knowledge puffs up. Love builds up. Without love, even the most impressive gifts amount to nothing.
Some in Corinth denied that the dead rise. Paul restates the gospel. Christ died, was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to many.
But Christ has indeed been raised from the dead.
His rising is the firstfruits of all who belong to him.

Some passages are hard, and faithful churches reach different answers: marriage, singleness, and divorce in chapter seven, head coverings in worship in chapter eleven, and gifts like tongues and the place of women in leading worship in chapters twelve to fourteen.
Readers weigh whether Paul grounds his words in creation, the gospel, or the custom of the day, and they weigh them differently. This film takes no side.
Start with chapters one to four, read as one piece.
Ask of each chapter: what has the crucified and risen Lord to do with this?
Paul's counsel near the end is short.
Do everything in love.
Second Corinthians is the most personal of Paul's letters. A visit had gone badly, and he had written in tears. Then Titus brought news that the church had turned back.
Paul writes in relief and joy, and in places in deep pain.
not to grieve you but to let you know how much I love you.
It has three parts. The ministry explained and the friendship mended. The collection for Jerusalem. And the fool's speech, where Paul boasts only of what shows his weakness.
Comfort, grace, and weakness are one gospel seen from three sides.
the Father of compassion and the God of all comfort
Corinth admired strength and polish. Paul says the gospel is treasure in jars of clay, to show that the power is God's.
Now we have this treasure in jars of clay to show that this surpassingly great power is from God and not from us.
He passes on the comfort he received, and comfort doesn't mean the trouble goes away.
To be reconciled is to be made friends again after a quarrel. God took the first step, reconciling the world to himself in Christ.
If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.
The letter is itself an act of reconciliation between a pastor and his people.
Paul never orders the church to give. He calls giving a grace, with Jesus, who became poor, as its pattern.
The gift is for the poor, not for Paul. And it gives no ground for teaching that giving to God will make the giver rich.
For God loves a cheerful giver.
Against rivals who prized polish, Paul boasts only of hardships, an escape in a basket, and a thorn God would not remove.
My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness.
His authority was for building up, not tearing down. A leader who uses this letter to demand loyalty has read it upside down.

Readers differ on whether this is one letter, or two or more joined together. Most often they propose that chapters ten to thirteen were once separate. Others note that no copy ever circulated in pieces. The argument can be followed on either view.
Scholars have long debated who the rival teachers were. This film takes no side. And it's not a letter against the Jewish people.
Read it in one sitting, aloud, as a real letter in the middle of a real quarrel.
Keep the story in mind, and watch for irony in chapters ten to thirteen.
who comforts us in all our troubles
Let it ask who you admire, and why.
Galatians is the most urgent of Paul's letters. Where a thanksgiving would go, he writes that he is amazed how quickly they are turning to a different gospel.
It's a short, fierce letter from a man afraid of losing people he loved.
I am amazed how quickly you are deserting the One who called you by the grace of Christ
It has three parts, with an opening and a closing in Paul's own hand.
First his own story. Then the argument from the Scriptures and from what the Galatians had seen. And last, freedom lived out.
a man is not justified by works of the law, but by faith in Jesus Christ.
Other teachers came. They were Jewish believers in Jesus, as Paul was, sincere in their faithfulness to God's word. They said Gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the law.
Paul answers that adding anything to Christ as the price of belonging changes the good news.
For if righteousness comes through the law, Christ died for nothing.
Paul argues from Israel's own Scriptures. Abraham believed God and was counted righteous, centuries before the law.
The law is God's good gift, a guardian until Christ came. Now all who belong to Christ are Abraham's heirs.
Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.
At Antioch, Peter stopped eating with Gentile believers, and Paul challenged him in front of everyone. For Paul, the gospel is at stake when believers refuse to eat together.
It was a quarrel among Jewish believers in Jesus, not between Christians and Jews.
For you are all one in Christ Jesus.
It is for freedom that Christ has set us free.

Freedom is for serving one another in love, not for self-indulgence. Paul sets the works of the flesh beside the fruit of the Spirit, and tells the churches to restore those who fall, gently, and to carry each other's burdens.
All Christians confess that no one is set right with God by circumcision or by the law. They read Paul's phrase works of the law in more than one way.

The traditional Protestant reading takes it as everything a person does to obey the law in order to stand right with God. The new perspective on Paul takes it above all as the practices that marked Jews off from other peoples. Many take something from both.
This film takes no side. And this letter is not against the Jewish people.
Read it in one sitting, aloud if you can, with Genesis open for chapters three and four. Don't stop at chapter four.
the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace
The letter asks what you are adding to Christ, quietly, as the price of belonging.

films.title: Ephesians: one new people in Christ

lines.text: Ephesians names Paul as its writer, in prison, to believers in Ephesus and the cities around it. It answers no crisis.
It steps back to look at the whole of what God is doing: a plan to bring all things in heaven and on earth together in Christ.
to bring all things in heaven and on earth together in Christ.
It has two halves, joined at the start of chapter four. Chapters one to three are praise, prayer, and teaching: what God has done. Chapters four to six are how to live because of it.
Cut the second half off from the first, and grace becomes a list of rules.
I urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling you have received
Salvation in Ephesians is God's work from first to last. The dead are made alive, by grace, through faith.
For it is by grace you have been saved through faith.
Faith is the way the gift is received, not a work that earns it. Yet believers are God's workmanship, made for the good works he prepared.
The deepest division of Paul's world, between Jew and Gentile, has been overcome in the cross. Gentiles once far off are brought near and joined to Israel's hope.
For He Himself is our peace, who has made the two one.
One new humanity. One household. One temple, where God lives by his Spirit.
Walk worthy. Tell the truth, deal with anger, work honestly, forgive.
Be kind and tenderhearted to one another, forgiving each other just as in Christ God forgave you.
The household passages put everyone under one Lord, and they lay demands on the strong. They give no one a license to control or harm another.
The letter takes spiritual evil seriously without making it the center. The struggle is not against flesh and blood. Christ is seated far above every power.
The believer's task is to stand, in the armor God supplies, and to pray.
Finally, be strong in the Lord and in His mighty power.

Churches today read the household passages differently, especially on marriage. Christians also read the letter's words on being chosen in different ways, and differ on whether Paul wrote it himself. On those questions this film takes no side.
All agree that the household passages call for mutual love, with Christ's self-giving as the pattern. Nothing in them asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger.
The words to slaves were misused for centuries to defend slavery. That misuse was wrong.
Read it slowly and whole, aloud if you can. The long opening sentences are praise, not tangled argument. Watch the hinge at chapter four.
The key chapters are one, two, four, five, and six.
Now to Him who is able to do immeasurably more than all we ask or imagine
Watch for these words: grace, in Christ, mystery, body, and walk.
Philippians is Paul's warmest letter. He writes from prison, facing a trial that could end in his death.
He writes to the church that had stood by him from the start, and had just sent him a gift by the hand of Epaphroditus.
I thank my God every time I remember you.
Thanks and news from prison. A call to stand together, with the hymn to Christ at its center. Knowing Christ, and pressing on. Then last appeals and thanks.
The hymn of chapter two shapes all that follows.
Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus
Words for joy come more than a dozen times in a letter written in chains.
Rejoice in the Lord always. I will say it again: Rejoice!
Paul's joy rests not on his circumstances but on the Lord. It has looked at suffering and death and not been undone.
At the letter's heart stands what many think was an early hymn. Christ, in the form of God, emptied himself, took the form of a servant, and was obedient to death on a cross. And God exalted him.
Humility here is the free choice to use one's place for others.
but emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant
Paul counts his impressive credentials as loss, to gain Christ and a righteousness from God through faith.
I count all things as loss compared to the surpassing excellence of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord.
He has not arrived. Like a runner, he presses on toward the goal.
Paul calls the church to pray instead of worrying. Then comes a much quoted line.
I can do all things through Christ who gives me strength.
In context it's not a promise of success. It's the strength to be content in hunger and in plenty.
Read it whole, as a letter between friends. It takes about fifteen minutes aloud. Watch the words joy, gospel, partnership, and mind.
Read chapter two slowly, and the famous line of chapter four with the verses around it.
And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding
It's a letter about joy, written in chains.
Colossians was written from prison to a small church Paul had never seen. Epaphras, one of its own people, had carried the gospel home.
Now some teaching promised more: visions, food rules, holy days, and attention to angels and powers.
You learned it from Epaphras, our beloved fellow servant
The first two chapters are about who Christ is, and the last two about how believers live. The turn comes at the start of chapter three.
The commands of the second half grow out of the gifts of the first.
since you have been raised with Christ, strive for the things above
Christ is the image of the invisible God. All things were made through him and for him.
He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together.
Firstborn means the heir with first place, not the first thing made, as the church confessed at Nicaea.
All the fullness of God dwells in Christ, and believers are complete in him.
Israel's feasts and Sabbaths were good gifts, a shadow pointing ahead, not a lie. The powers people feared were disarmed at the cross.
These are a shadow of the things to come, but the body that casts it belongs to Christ.
Believers put off the old self, with its anger, greed, and lies. They put on compassion, kindness, patience, and forgiveness.
And over all these virtues put on love, which is the bond of perfect unity.
In the renewed self there is no Greek or Jew, slave or free. Christ is all.
Paul puts every relationship in the Lord. He speaks to the weaker first, and lays duties, not privileges, on the stronger.

Churches read the words to wives and husbands differently. All agree they give no one a license to control or harm another, and nothing in them asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger.
The words to slaves were misused for centuries to defend slavery. That misuse was wrong.
Whatever you do, work at it with your whole being, for the Lord and not for men

Christians differ on who wrote the letter. Paul himself, as the letter says and the early church received it. A follower of Paul after his death, as many scholars since the eighteen hundreds have argued. Or Timothy during Paul's life, with his approval.
This film takes no side.
Read it in one sitting, aloud if you can. Then read the song of Christ slowly, more than once.
Let it ask whether you have treated Christ as a good beginning, and looked elsewhere for the rest.
And you have been made complete in Christ.

films.title: 1 Thessalonians: hope that does not give up

lines.text: First Thessalonians is very likely the oldest of Paul's letters to survive, written around the year fifty.
Forced to leave by night, he had left a few new believers facing hard neighbors. Timothy brings good news, and Paul writes in relief.
Timothy has returned from his visit with the good news
The first half looks back: thanks for their faith, love, and hope, and how Paul lived among them. The second looks ahead: holiness, love, quiet work, and the Lord's coming.
Every chapter ends near the same place.
your work of faith, your labor of love, and your enduring hope
Most of these believers had worshiped idols until a few weeks before, and they turned to serve the living and true God.
Paul lived among them, gentle as a nursing mother and caring as a father, working night and day so as not to be a burden.
how you turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God
Some believers had died, and the living feared they had missed the Lord's coming. Paul doesn't tell them not to grieve.
He tells them not to grieve like those without hope, because Jesus died and rose again.
And so we will always be with the Lord.

Every Christian tradition confesses that Jesus will come again and the dead will be raised. Christians differ on the order of events, and on whether being caught up is a separate rapture. This film takes no side.
Paul gives no date.
The Day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night.
So no one should set a date, or name a living person, a nation, or an event of our own day as what these verses describe.
The letter ends with short commands for life together. Respect leaders. Care for the weak. Rejoice. Pray. Give thanks. Test everything.
Waiting for the Lord means living well among your neighbors, not leaving them behind.
Pray without ceasing.
Read it in one sitting, as a pastor's letter to new believers he loves. Read the end of chapter four for what Paul says it's for.
Therefore encourage one another with these words.
Whom are you grieving, and where is your hope?
Hebrews begins like a sermon and ends like a letter, and no one knows who wrote it.
It was written to believers who had once suffered bravely, and were now tired, drifting, and tempted to give up on Christ.
But in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son
Teaching and urging take turns. Jesus is greater than the angels and Moses. He is a high priest like Melchizedek, and the one offering the tabernacle pointed toward.
From chapter ten, the call is to draw near and endure.
the covenant He mediates is better and is founded on better promises.
God, who spoke through the prophets, has spoken last and best in his Son.
The Son is the radiance of God’s glory and the exact representation of His nature.
The Son is also fully human: made like his brothers, tempted, crying out with tears.
The word better runs through the book. The old covenant is a shadow, not because it was false, but because it pointed ahead. The writer honors it as God's gift.
This book was misused to teach contempt for the Jewish people. That misuse was wrong.
For the law is only a shadow of the good things to come
Hebrews alone calls Jesus a priest at length. He offered not animals but himself, once for all, and sat down because the work was finished.
He was tempted in every way, yet without sin, so he can sympathize.
He always lives to intercede for them.

Five solemn warnings not to drift or turn away run beside as many words of hope. They're addressed to people the writer believes will persevere. How they relate to assurance is much debated, and this film takes no side.
