Then come the roll call of faith, and the race.
Let us fix our eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of our faith.
Start with chapter one, then eleven and twelve. The key chapters are one, two, four, six, seven, nine, eleven, and twelve.
Read with the Old Testament texts it builds on open beside it, and watch for the word better.
Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.
James reads less like an argument than a string of sharp, practical sayings from a pastor who has watched faith go soft.
The church has long held that its writer was the brother of Jesus, who once did not believe and became a leader in Jerusalem.
James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ
Look for threads rather than a tidy outline: trials, wisdom, wealth, speech, faith and deeds, taken up again and again from new angles.
It sounds like Proverbs, and still more like the Sermon on the Mount.
Be doers of the word, and not hearers only.
James opens by calling trials an occasion for joy. Not because suffering is good, but because tested faith produces perseverance, and perseverance leads to maturity.
He's honest that trials hurt, and he insists that God tempts no one and gives only good gifts.
the testing of your faith develops perseverance.
Faith that does nothing is dead. It's the faith of bare words, which tells the hungry to keep warm and gives nothing.
So too, faith by itself, if it does not result in action, is dead.

Paul and James both teach that God saves by grace and that true faith is alive. They use faith, works, and justify in different senses. Christians relate the two in several ways, and this film takes no side.
Few books speak so sharply about wealth. James condemns giving the best seats to the rich, warns the rich that they fade like a flower, and pronounces woe on those who hold back wages.
God has chosen the poor.
Has not God chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith
Every chapter touches the tongue. A small spark sets a great forest ablaze. Speech is the clearest test of whether faith has reached the whole person.
Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger.
Read all five chapters at one sitting. It takes about fifteen minutes. Watch the threads, and read it beside the Sermon on the Mount.
The key chapters are one, two, three, and five.
he should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault
James wants a faith that works.
First Peter is a letter of hope to believers who had become strangers in their own towns. They had left the festivals that held town life together, and were insulted and slandered.
They had not lost their homes, but they had lost their place.
as foreigners and exiles
It has four movements. Who you are. How to live among neighbors who slander you. Suffering for doing good. And a word to elders and to all.
One pattern runs through it, first for Christ and then for his people: suffering now, and glory after.
after you have suffered for a little while, the God of all grace
God has given new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus. An inheritance waits that cannot spoil.
Trials test faith, more precious than gold, and they are a short time before glory.
a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead
Peter gives a mostly Gentile church the titles God gave Israel at Sinai.
But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation.
He is a Jew, writing in Israel's own Scriptures to welcome Gentiles into Israel's blessings. Using the New Testament to justify contempt for Jews is false.
To suffer for doing good, without striking back, is to walk where Christ walked. Peter's readers neither retaliate nor retreat. They do good and give a gentle answer.
These chapters never say that someone being harmed must stay and bear it.
When they heaped abuse on Him, He did not retaliate
Elders are to shepherd God's flock willingly, as examples. Everyone is to be humble.
Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you.
Peter doesn't tell sufferers to carry it alone. After a little while, the God of all grace will restore them.

Christians differ on who wrote the letter, on how Israel and the church fit together, on Christ's preaching to the spirits in prison, and on how the words to wives and husbands apply today. On those this film takes no side.
Using Peter's words to slaves to defend slavery was a misuse, and it was wrong.
Read it in one sitting, as a real letter to frightened people. Read the household passages beside the picture of Christ in chapter two.
Where churches differ, read more than one view before you settle.
the reason for the hope that is in you.
Suffering now, and glory after.

films.title: 1 John: so that you may know

lines.text: First John reads like a sermon written down, with no greeting and no named writer.
A group had left these churches, taking a new teaching about Jesus, and those who stayed wondered whether they really knew God. John writes to steady them.
They went out from us, but they did not belong to us.
John works like a composer with a few themes: light, love, truth, obedience, and belief. He comes back to each from a new angle.
God is light, and in Him there is no darkness at all.
The letter begins with witnesses who heard, saw, and touched the Word of life. Against teachers who said the divine Christ only seemed to have a body, John insists he came in the flesh.
A spirituality that despises the body soon despises the neighbor.
which we have seen with our own eyes, which we have gazed upon and touched with our own hands
Three marks keep returning: believing the truth about Jesus, keeping God's commands, and loving one another. John won't let them be pulled apart.
They were written to steady people, not to make tender consciences anxious.
By this we can be sure that we have come to know Him: if we keep His commandments.
John holds two truths together. Anyone who says he has no sin deceives himself, and God forgives and cleanses those who confess.
He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
Yet a child of God doesn't settle into sin. Don't deny your sin, and don't make peace with it.
God is love, and love is defined by what God did: he sent his Son. So love is concrete, laying down one's life and opening the hand to a brother in need.
Perfect love drives out the dread of judgment.
Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love.
Christians differ on who wrote the letter, on how to read the words that a child of God does not keep on sinning, and on how assurance works. This film takes no side.
The letter's antichrists were teachers who denied that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh, and this film names no one living today.
Read it in one sitting, aloud if you can, with John's Gospel open beside it. Remember the split behind it.
And let it ask where your confidence before God rests.
John writes so that you may know that you have eternal life.

films.title: Revelation: the Lamb on the throne

lines.text: Revelation is the last book of the Bible. Its title means an unveiling.
It was written to real churches under real pressure, some in danger, some comfortable and compromised. It shows them their world as heaven sees it.
Do not be afraid. I am the First and the Last.
John sees the risen Christ and receives messages for seven churches. Then a door opens in heaven: God's throne, and a Lamb who opens a sealed scroll.
A sequence of visions follows, and the book ends with a new heaven and a new earth.
Blessed is the one who reads aloud the words of this prophecy
The throne is the book's central image. Whatever chaos appears on earth, the vision of chapter four shows the One seated on the throne, worshiped day and night.
The empires that claim ultimate power are not ultimate.
Holy, Holy, Holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come!
John hears of the Lion of the tribe of Judah. He looks, and sees a Lamb who was slain. That reversal defines the book.
Worthy is the Lamb, who was slain.
Christ conquers by sacrifice, and his people overcome the same way.
Readers follow four main approaches. Some read most of it as fulfilled in the first centuries. Some as a map of church history. Some as events still to come. Some as the conflict of every age.
Many combine them, and faithful Christians hold each. This film takes no side and names no date.
Here is a call for the perseverance of the saints

Revelation doesn't flinch from judgment on evil, but it doesn't end there. The goal is a renewed creation in which God dwells with his people, death is gone, and the nations walk in the light of the Lamb.
He will wipe away every tear from their eyes.
Start with chapter one. The key chapters are one, two, five, twelve, thirteen, twenty, twenty-one, and twenty-two.
Read its symbols by the Old Testament. The book's own interest is less in timetables than in worship, endurance, and hope.
Come, Lord Jesus!

films.title: Who God is: Father, Son and Holy Spirit

lines.text: The Bible begins where Israel began, with Israel's daily confession.
Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One.
Jesus called it the most important commandment. The first Christians were Jews who prayed these words, and they never stopped. There is one God and no other.
Paul takes Israel's own confession and speaks of one God, the Father, from whom all things came and for whom we exist. The Father is God.
The Bible gives no picture of him, and this film doesn't draw one. Jesus taught his followers to pray to our Father in heaven.
yet for us there is but one God, the Father, from whom all things came and for whom we exist.
John opens his Gospel this way.
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
With God, and God. When Thomas meets the risen Jesus behind locked doors, he calls him my Lord and my God. The Son is fully God, and in Jesus he also became fully man.
The Spirit is not a force God uses. The Bible speaks of him as God. When Ananias lied to the Holy Spirit, Peter told him he had not lied to men, but to God.
And the Spirit is everywhere, as only God is.
Where can I go to escape Your Spirit? Where can I flee from Your presence?
At the Jordan the three are seen together, and none of them is the other. The Son comes up out of the water. The Spirit descends on him like a dove. And the Father speaks from heaven.
You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased.
The Father is not the Son, and the Son is not the Spirit.
The risen Jesus sends his followers out, baptizing in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. One name.
Christians say God is one in being and three in persons, each fully God, and one God. Or more simply: one what, three whos.
Not three gods. Not one person in three masks. Not three parts.
baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit
Every picture from inside the world breaks, and each teaches an old mistake. Water as ice, liquid, and steam is one thing in three forms. That's one person in three masks.
A clover makes each person a third of God, when each is wholly God. Three people sharing one nature would be three gods. The church weighed these long ago and set them aside.
To whom will you liken God? To what image will you compare Him?
So instead of a picture, Christians keep the Bible's words and the creed's. The Nicene Creed calls the Son God of God, Light of Light, very God of very God.
The family catechism calls this not a riddle to solve but a wonder to receive. God has always been love.
The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with all of you.

films.title: Creation and the image of God

lines.text: In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.
Genesis opens with God already there. Nothing comes before him, and nothing helps him.
Christians confess that God made all things, seen and unseen, out of nothing, by the word of his power.
Day by day the empty world is given shape and then filled. Six times God calls what he made good. The seventh time, very good.
The world is not a mistake or a prison. It's a gift.
And God looked upon all that He had made, and indeed, it was very good.
People come last, and they are different. In the ancient world a king could be called the image of a god. Genesis gives that dignity to every person, male and female, not only to kings.
So God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them.
Being made in God's image means we were made to know him, to reflect his character, and to rule over and care for his world as those who answer to him.
We were made for God himself.
everyone called by My name and created for My glory, whom I have indeed formed and made.
Image and work arrive together. God blesses the man and the woman and gives them the earth to rule and to care for on his behalf.
To tend it and keep it, not to spoil it for themselves.
Then the LORD God took the man and placed him in the Garden of Eden to cultivate and keep it.
The image is given, not earned. A newborn, a man with advanced dementia, and the most gifted adult in the room have the same worth, because their worth was never a ranking of what they can do.
Many who don't believe in God hold the same belief, and live it well.
You crowned him with glory and honor.
That God created, that he created from nothing, and that humanity bears his image are what all Christians confess.

The age of the earth and the way God created are open questions, and faithful Christians who love the same Bible have landed in different places. This film takes no side on the age of the earth or on evolution.
We were made for God himself.
Jesus summed up what God asks in two commands. Love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, mind, and strength. And love your neighbor as yourself.
Made for that love, people were joined to God, to each other, to themselves, and to the world he gave them.
Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.
In Genesis three, the serpent doesn't start with the fruit. He starts by making God sound mean. Then he makes a promise: you will be like God.
At its root, sin is not trusting that God is good, and wanting to be our own god, deciding good and evil for ourselves.
The damage runs in every direction at once. They hide from God. They cover their shame. They blame each other. And the ground grows thorns.
Isaiah says it plainly. Your iniquities have built barriers between you and your God.
The family catechism defines it. Sin is any failure to love God and others as we should, whether by doing what God forbids or by failing to do what he commands.
It's more than a list of wrong things done. It's love turned in on ourselves.
Paul says it without exception.
For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.
No one is outside it and no one is above it, the people who wrote the Bible included. But the same sentence goes straight on to grace.
Judgment is never the only word. God comes looking and calls: where are you? Jesus said he came to seek and to save the lost. At the cross God himself mends what sin broke.
And the way home stays open.
If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins.
All Christians confess that every person has sinned and needs God's grace, and that God himself comes to save.
How the first sin reaches everyone after it is debated, and churches word it differently. This film doesn't choose between them.
The way home stays open.
John begins before the beginning.
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
The Son did not begin at Bethlehem. Through him all things were made.
The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us.
He didn't stop being God when he became man, and he didn't only seem to be a man. He took a real human nature. He was born, he grew, he learned.
The Gospels don't hide his humanity. Weary from walking, he sits down by a well. At his friend's tomb, Jesus wept.
Hebrews says he was tempted in every way that we are, yet without sin.
we have one who was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin.
In Mark he tells a paralyzed man that his sins are forgiven, and the scribes object: who can forgive sins but God alone?
He rebukes the wind and the sea, and his friends ask the question.
Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?
Not half God and half man. Not a man who became God. Not God dressed up as a man.
The church confessed it at the Council of Chalcedon in the year four fifty-one: one person who is truly God and truly man. Fully God and fully man, in one person, forever.
For in Christ all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form.
Only someone who is both could bring God and people back together.
As man he could stand in our place. As God he could carry what no one else could.
He had to be made like His brothers in every way
Near Caesarea Philippi, after hearing what others said, Jesus asked: who do you say I am? Peter answered.
You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.
Some say he was only a good teacher. The Honest Answer on that question weighs it.
One person, truly God and truly man.
The creed says he was crucified also for us under Pontius Pilate. The chief priests and their council handed him over. Pilate, the Roman governor, condemned him. Roman soldiers crucified him.

Jesus himself, his disciples, and the first church were Jews, and blaming the Jewish people for his death is a lie that Christians must reject plainly. The New Testament places all of us inside the guilt.
that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures
At the first Passover a lamb died in the place of the firstborn, and Israel went free. Jesus died at Passover, and Paul says it.
For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.
A ransom was the price paid to set a slave or a prisoner free.
For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many.
Peter says the price was not silver or gold but Christ himself. He paid it with his own life, freely given.
Isaiah saw a servant who suffered for others.
The punishment that brought us peace was upon Him.
This is not an angry Father against an unwilling Son. Jesus said he lays his life down of his own accord. The one who bears it is God himself in the Son.
Many early Christian writers loved this picture. By his death Jesus broke the power of the one who holds the power of death, and set free those held in slavery by their fear of death.
He disarmed the powers, triumphing over them by the cross.
triumphing over them by the cross
But God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
The cross does not change God's heart toward us. It shows it. Some Christians put this picture at the center: the love seen at the cross changes those who see it.
Reconciled was the word for making peace between people at war.
Here the one who was wronged, God, makes peace and pays the cost himself.
God was reconciling the world to Himself in Christ
No one picture says it all. Christians hold them together, and some traditions put one at the center. The creed doesn't choose a theory. It says he came for us men and for our salvation.
Christians read Isaiah's servant as Jesus, and many Jewish readers read him as the people of Israel. This film doesn't choose between the ways of explaining the cross.
And the cross is not the end of the story. On the third day the tomb was empty.
that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures
Christians confess that Jesus died and was buried. Joseph of Arimathea, a disciple, laid the body in his own new tomb cut into the rock, and rolled a great stone across the entrance.
The summary Paul passed on puts the burial between the death and the rising, because the one who was raised is the one who was buried.
that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures

Very early on the first day of the week, the women came with the spices they had prepared. They found the stone rolled away, and they did not find the body. All four Gospels tell of the empty tomb that morning.
The question they were asked is the whole story in one sentence.
Why do you look for the living among the dead? He is not here; He has risen!

John tells of Mary Magdalene weeping outside the tomb. She took the risen Jesus for the gardener until he said her name. He sent her to his brothers with a message, and she went and told the disciples.
I have seen the Lord!
The first news of Easter was a message to be carried.
The risen Jesus is not a ghost or a memory. He told his frightened friends to look at his hands and feet, and he ate broiled fish in front of them.
Yet his body was also changed. He came among them behind locked doors, and he was not always recognized at first. Christians confess that God raised the same body that had been buried, now made new.
Look at My hands and My feet. It is I Myself.
Jesus had called Lazarus out of his tomb, still bound in strips of linen, back to the life he had before. Jesus' own rising was different. He was raised into a life on the far side of death.
Death no longer has dominion over Him.
Under the law, Israel brought the first sheaf of the harvest to the priest: the first sheaf, and the promise of the rest. Paul uses that picture for Easter.
But Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.

Paul says that if Christ has not been raised, faith is futile. Because he was raised, the forgiveness won at the cross is sealed, death is not the final word over anyone who belongs to him, and the body and the world God made matter.
Every Sunday gathering is a small Easter. It doesn't take away grief. It gives grief a hope.
Because I live, you also will live.
The story starts with a gift, not a problem. God made human beings in his own image, to know him and show what he is like, and to love him and be happy in him forever.
Nothing stood between people and God.
So God created man in His own image
People turned from God to their own way, and every one of us has followed.
Sin is more than a list of wrong things done. It's a break: with God, with each other, inside ourselves.
for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God
Every age builds its towers: be good enough, try harder, earn your way back. The Bible says plainly that the gap is too wide.
Salvation is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast.
That's hard news for anyone who likes to earn things, and good news for anyone who knows they can't.
Then God crosses the gap from his own side. The Father sends the Son, not to win over an unwilling God, but because he already loves the world.
For God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son, that everyone who believes in Him shall not perish but have eternal life.
The eternal Son becomes one of us, fully God and fully man.
At the cross the break is mended, and God is the one who mends it. The Father and the Son are not on opposite sides here.
For Christ also suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God.
He was buried, and on the third day he was raised, in his body, not as an idea.
The resurrection is God's sign that the cross did what it set out to do.
He was delivered over to death for our trespasses and was raised to life for our justification.
The gift is received, not earned. Jesus said to repent and believe in the gospel: turn around, and trust him.
Faith is not a work that pays for anything. It's empty hands taking what is given.
Repent and believe in the gospel!
God gives more than a clean record. Those who belong to Christ are forgiven, adopted as God's children, given the Holy Spirit, and joined to his people.
If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.
All Christians confess that sinners are saved by God's grace, through Jesus' death and resurrection, and not by their own good deeds.
Churches differ on the place of baptism, on how God's choosing and our choosing fit together, and on whether a believer can fall away. This film doesn't choose between them.
The story ends where it began, with God and his people together, and more than before. Christians differ on many details of the last things. On this hope they speak together.
and there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain

films.title: Grace: the gift no one earns

lines.text: A wage is owed. A gift is not. The Bible's word for the gift is grace: the free and undeserved favor of God, who gives sinners what they could never earn and forgives what they could never repay.
For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.
Jesus told of a landowner who paid those who had worked one hour the same as those who had worked twelve. The early workers grumbled, and he answered that he had wronged no one.
Or are you envious because I am generous?
Grace offends anyone who is keeping count.
Grace is not God grading on a curve. He didn't wait for sinners to put things right.
He paid the debt himself, while we were still his enemies. The cross is what the gift cost.
But God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
So salvation is received, never achieved: by grace, through faith, not by works.
Faith is not the one good deed that earns it. Faith is the empty hand that takes what is given.
For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast.
Does that make sin safe? Paul heard the question and answered it at once.
Shall we continue in sin so that grace may increase? Certainly not!
The grace that forgives also teaches. Good works are not the root of salvation. They are its fruit.
And grace doesn't stop at the door. Paul pleaded three times for a weakness to be taken away, and it was not. He was given this instead.
My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness.
Grace enough for the day, and God's power at its clearest where ours runs out.
The gift is meant to travel. People who know they have been forgiven, forgive. People who know that everything they have was given, give.
In the church no one has anything they did not receive.
Be kind and tenderhearted to one another, forgiving each other just as in Christ God forgave you.
All Christians confess that salvation is God's gift, received by grace and not earned.
They differ on how God's grace and the human will relate, and on how grace is received: by faith alone, or by faith with the sacraments and the life of the church. This film takes no side.
Grace is the gift that no one earns.

films.title: Faith: trusting the one who promised

lines.text: Faith, in the Bible's sense, is trust in God and in what he has promised. It's not a leap in the dark, and it doesn't grow stronger the less evidence it has.
It's the answer a person gives to someone who has spoken and has proved reliable.
Now faith is the assurance of what we hope for and the certainty of what we do not see.
Abraham is the pattern. Old and childless, he was told his family would be like the stars, and he believed, centuries before the law.
Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness.
The same Abraham also doubted and schemed. Biblical faith is not a flawless mood. It's reliance that is tested and deepened.
In the Gospels, faith is not a force the believer generates. It's reliance on Jesus himself, which is why a mustard seed of it is enough.
Its strength was never in the believing. It's in the one believed.
Let us fix our eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of our faith
A father brought his suffering son to Jesus, and prayed one of the most honest prayers in the Gospels.
I do believe; help my unbelief!
His faith was mixed and struggling, and Jesus answered it. Doubt brought to Jesus is still coming to Jesus.
Faith grows the way trust between persons grows: by hearing and remembering what the other has said and done.
That's why Scripture keeps retelling the exodus, and why Paul ties faith to hearing the word.
Consequently, faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of Christ.
The Bible's word for faith is also its word for faithfulness, so trust doesn't stay private. It obeys, endures, and keeps its promises.
Churches describe the link between faith and works in different words, and none of them teaches that faith earns salvation. This film takes no side.
So too, faith by itself, if it does not result in action, is dead.
Hebrews eleven is a list of people who acted on what God had said without seeing the outcome. Many died still waiting.
Faith doesn't deny the darkness. It holds to the one who has spoken in it, and walks on.
For we walk by faith, not by sight.
Its strength is in the one believed.
The story starts with a gift, not a problem. God made human beings in his own image, to know him and to love him forever. Nothing stood between people and God.
People turned from God to their own way, and every one of us has followed. Sin is a break: with God, with each other, inside ourselves.
Every age builds its towers: be good enough, try harder, earn your way back. The gap is too wide for us to cross.
Then God crosses the gap from his own side. The Father sends the Son because he loves the world, and the Son becomes one of us, fully God and fully man.
At the cross the break is mended, and God is the one who mends it. Jesus died for our sins, and on the third day he was raised, in his body.
that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures
The gift is received, not earned. Turn around, and trust him. Faith is not a work that pays for anything. It's empty hands taking what is given.
Those who belong to Christ are forgiven, made God's children, and given new life, now and in the life to come.
Read more on LiveWell, or talk it over with a pastor or someone you trust.

films.title: The Holy Spirit in a believer

lines.text: The Holy Spirit is the third person of the Trinity, fully God, who dwells in believers and gives them life with God.
He is not a force or a feeling. He is God himself, living in his people.
And if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to Christ.
The Spirit unites believers to Christ. Jesus' own picture is a vine and its branches. The branch lives because it is joined to the vine.
I am the vine and you are the branches.
Apart from him they can do nothing.
To be adopted means God makes people his own children, with a sure place in his family.
Paul says God sent the Spirit of his Son into their hearts, calling out to God as Father. Abba is the Aramaic word for father.
God sent the Spirit of His Son into our hearts
This is the lifelong work of the Spirit, by which believers grow to be more like Jesus. Paul names nine kinds of fruit.
But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control.
Fruit grows slowly, and it grows because the branch is joined to the vine.
The Spirit gives gifts to each believer, and they are given for the good of all: teaching, serving, encouraging, giving, leading, showing mercy.
Paul's picture is the body, where every part is needed.
Now to each one the manifestation of the Spirit is given for the common good.
Christians agree that the Holy Spirit is God, gives new life, lives in every believer, and gives gifts to build up the church.

Churches differ on whether some gifts, such as tongues, prophecy, and healing, continue as they did in Acts, and on whether the baptism of the Spirit is a distinct experience after a person first believes. This film doesn't choose between them.
Even prayer is not left to believers alone. When they don't know how to pray, the Spirit himself intercedes for them.
The Spirit helps us in our weakness.
The Spirit is not a reward for the strong. He is help for the weak.
He is God himself, living in his people.
The church is the whole company of God's people, gathered by the Spirit around Christ, called to worship God, love one another, and make him known to the world.
A building is only where some of them meet.
Paul's picture is a body: many parts, different gifts, one life.
No part can say it doesn't need the others, and none is a spare.
The body is a unit, though it is composed of many parts.
Peter's picture is a house of living stones. God is building his people into a dwelling for himself, and the stone the whole house rests on is Christ.
you also, like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house
God saves us into a family, not alone.
Strangers become members of one household, brothers and sisters who help one another follow Jesus all the way home.
They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and to the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer.
That was the first church in Jerusalem. Christians still gather to worship God, hear his Word, share the Lord's Supper, and help one another.
The church is gathered to be sent. Jesus' last command was to make disciples of all nations, and his last promise was his own presence to the end of the age.
And surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age.
Churches share the confession of one Lord and the command to baptize in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

They differ on who should be baptized and how, and on how churches are led: by bishops, by elders, or by the congregation deciding together. Faithful churches differ on these while confessing one Lord, and this film doesn't choose between them.
one Lord, one faith, one baptism
The church is a people, gathered to be sent.
Jesus' last command to his disciples included baptism: make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
From the church's first day, those who received the message were baptized.
Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit

Paul passes on what he received. On the night he was betrayed, the Lord Jesus took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and said it was his body, given for them: do this in remembrance of me. The cup, he said, is the new covenant in his blood.
For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until He comes.
Both point to the same thing: Jesus' death and resurrection. Paul says believers were buried with Christ through baptism so that they may walk in newness of life.
Churches agree that repentance, faith, and baptism belong together in the New Testament, and that the Supper is received with self-examination and love.
we too may walk in newness of life.
Some churches baptize the children of believers, pointing to Peter's promise to you and your children.

Others, Baptists and many evangelicals among them, baptize only those who confess faith for themselves, noting that in Acts those who received the message were baptized. Both read the same chapters carefully.
This promise belongs to you and your children and to all who are far off
Some churches pour or sprinkle water. Others immerse, taking the person under the water and up again, a picture of burial and rising.
Churches also differ on what baptism does. Catholic, Orthodox, and Lutheran Christians hold it to be a sacrament through which God grants forgiveness and the Spirit.
Reformed and Presbyterian churches call it a sign and seal of the covenant of grace. Baptists and many evangelicals call it an ordinance, the commanded public sign that follows faith.
Roman Catholic teaching holds that the bread and wine become Christ's body and blood. Lutherans confess Christ's true body and blood present in, with, and under the bread and wine.
Reformed churches teach a real spiritual feeding on Christ by faith. Many Baptist and free churches stress a memorial meal of remembrance and proclamation.
All agree that the meal proclaims the Lord's death until he comes.
Paul writes of one Lord, one faith, one baptism. Faithful churches differ on these questions while confessing that one Lord, and this film doesn't choose between them.
How your own church practices baptism and the Supper, and why, is a good question to bring to a parent or a pastor.
Both point to Jesus' death and resurrection.

films.title: The Bible: how we got it

lines.text: The Bible's books were written over many centuries, in palaces and in exile, in prison cells and on the road.

Their writers include kings, priests, prophets, court officials, a tax collector, a physician, fishermen, and a former Pharisee. Many books name no author at all. Christians believe God was at work in the whole of it.
On many past occasions and in many different ways, God spoke to our fathers through the prophets.
Prophets spoke and helpers wrote. Baruch wrote on a scroll all the words Jeremiah dictated, and when the king burned that scroll, Jeremiah dictated it again.
Paul usually dictated his letters to a secretary and added a greeting in his own hand. One of those secretaries signs his own name in Romans.
I, Tertius, who wrote down this letter, greet you in the Lord.
Books were written on scrolls of papyrus or of prepared animal skin, in ink, with a reed pen.
The Old Testament is in Hebrew, with a small part in Aramaic, a related language. The New Testament is in Greek. Paul once asked a friend to bring him his scrolls, especially the parchments.
my scrolls, especially the parchments.
Copies were made almost at once. Paul asked one church to pass its letter on to another, and to read the one sent there.
Every copy was made by hand until printing came, and every hand-made copy differs from every other in small ways. That's why scholars compare the copies.
After this letter has been read among you, make sure that it is also read in the church of the Laodiceans
From very early on, Christians preferred the codex, a book of folded sheets stitched at the spine, to the scroll.

It was cheaper, since it used both sides of the sheet. It was easier to carry and to search. And it could hold all four Gospels, or all of Paul's letters, in one volume. Nearly all early Christian copies are books of this kind.
The churches received as Scripture the books that came from the apostles and their circle, taught the faith handed on in all the churches, and were read in worship across the Christian world.
Behind those tests was the conviction that the church was recognizing books that had already proved themselves.
Christians of different traditions account for this differently, and Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include further books in the Old Testament. This film doesn't choose between them.
Translation is part of the Bible's own story. The New Testament itself puts some of Jesus' Aramaic words into Greek.
Jews made the Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures that the first churches outside Judea read, and the New Testament was in Latin, Syriac, and Coptic by the third century.
Every translation is a set of decisions, which is why it helps to read more than one.
All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness.
Prayer is talking with God, who is our Father: bringing him worship, thanks, confession, and requests, and trusting that he hears because of Jesus.
It's not a way of getting things out of God. It's a child speaking to a father.

When his disciples asked him to teach them to pray, Jesus gave them a pattern, the Lord's Prayer. God's name honored. His kingdom and his will first. Then daily bread, forgiveness as we forgive, and protection from evil.
Your kingdom come, Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.
Christians all over the world still pray it.
Praise tells God who he is. Thanks tells him what he has done.
The psalms, the Bible's own book of prayers and songs, are full of both.
Enter His gates with thanksgiving and His courts with praise
Paul tells worried people not to swallow their worry but to turn it into prayer, with thanks.
Be anxious for nothing, but in everything, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God.
Asking is not bothering God. It's what children do with a father who loves them.
Confession is neither groveling nor hiding. When we sin we confess it to God, who is faithful and just to forgive us because of Jesus, and we turn from it.
There is no sin too big for the cross.
If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins
Prayer is not a promise that we will get what we ask. Jesus himself asked his Father in the garden to take the cup of suffering away, and added these words.
Yet not My will, but Yours be done.
Some prayers, even for someone to get better, are not answered the way we longed for, and that hurts. The Bible doesn't hide it. Many of its prayers ask God: how long, O LORD?
Paul says that when we don't know how we ought to pray, the Spirit himself prays for us, with groans too deep for words.
Prayer doesn't depend on finding the right words. It rests on God, who wants to hear.
the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groans too deep for words.
It's a child speaking to a father.
Here's an objection you may have heard. We don't have the original New Testament. Not one page.
Only copies of copies, made by hand for centuries. So how could anyone know what it first said?
Start with what's true, because a lot of it is.
The New Testament was copied by hand for nearly fifteen hundred years, until it was first printed in Greek in 1516.
None of the originals survives. And the copies differ from one another in more places than there are words in the New Testament.
But think about why that number is so big.
Every copyist made mistakes. So the more copies survive, the more mistakes survive with them. And no book of the ancient world survives in more copies than this one.
Compare one of Rome's great histories. The first six books of the Annals of Tacitus survive in a single medieval copy.
One copy has no differences to count. That doesn't make it more reliable. It makes its mistakes invisible.
So what are all those differences?
Most are spelling and simple slips. A letter dropped. A word written twice.
Many more you couldn't even see in English, like the order of words in a Greek sentence.
Some change the meaning, but turn up in one late copy against all the rest.
And a small share both change the meaning and have a real claim to be original. One leading scholar puts them at less than one percent.
Here's one of those hard cases. Jesus is speaking about the day He will return.
No one knows about that day or hour, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.
The oldest copies of Matthew have the words, nor the Son. Many later copies leave them out, most likely because they were hard to explain.
And that's how we know. The older wording didn't vanish. It survived in other copies, right beside the change.
That's why the telephone game is the wrong picture. In that game, one whisper passes down one line, and nobody can check it.
The New Testament was written, not whispered. And it was copied in many places at once, from Egypt to Gaul, by people who never met.
A mistake made in one branch is passed down that branch and nowhere else. Lay the branches side by side, and the mistake stands out.
Older copies stayed in use, too. A copy of Luke and John from about the year two hundred agrees closely with a great Bible made more than a century later.
And the church argued about differences in the open. Around the year one eighty, Irenaeus said the oldest copies of Revelation read six hundred sixty-six, not six hundred sixteen.
Those are people checking, not people whispering.
There are honest limits, and you should hear them.
The earliest pieces we have are small, and their dates are argued over. The first stretch of copying is the part no one can see.

And Christians have sometimes claimed too much. A fragment of Mark was once announced as first century. It turned out to be from the late second or early third, and the scholar who announced it apologized in public.
Still, to hide in those early years, a change would have had to spread everywhere and erase the older wording in every branch. That's possible. It isn't the likeliest story.
Now set the New Testament beside the other books of its world.
Homer's Iliad, the best-kept classical work, survives in about seventeen hundred and fifty manuscripts.
The earliest copies of Julius Caesar's war in Gaul were made about nine hundred years after he wrote it.
Historians quote those books every day, and they should. And on any honest count, the New Testament has more copies, in more languages, closer to its writing, than any of them.
So here's where the evidence lands. We know what the New Testament says with high confidence in nearly every place. And where we don't, we know that we don't.
Even Bart Ehrman, the skeptic who made that big number famous, has said the essential Christian beliefs don't rest on a disputed reading.
But knowing what Matthew wrote doesn't tell you whether it happened. That's a different question, and it deserves its own answer.
The grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of our God stands forever.
So open it. Read it slowly. Then ask whether it's true.
Here's another objection. The Gospels were written decades after Jesus, by people who never met Him, under names someone added later.
If that's true, why trust what they say?
Again, start with what's true.
Jesus was crucified around the year thirty. Most scholars date Mark around seventy, Matthew and Luke later, and John in the nineties.
That's forty to sixty-five years. Some able scholars argue for earlier dates, but that's a minority view, and it has to be argued, not assumed.
And none of the four Gospels names its author in its own text.
But think about what a gap like that is. It sits inside a single lifetime.
People who had known Jesus were still alive. Many more had known them.
And we have writing from inside the gap. Paul's letters, from the fifties.
In one of them, Paul passes on a summary he says he himself received.

For what I received I passed on to you as of first importance: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures,
Most scholars, including many with no stake in Christianity, think that summary took shape within a few years of the cross.
And Paul says he stayed fifteen days with Peter in Jerusalem, and later met James and John.
Historians of the ancient world work with far bigger gaps than this.
One of our main accounts of Alexander the Great's campaigns, by Arrian, was written more than four centuries after them. Historians still use it, carefully.
So the question isn't only how long the gap was. It's what stood inside it.
Now the names. It's true the titles, According to Matthew and the rest, were almost certainly added by others.
But anonymous isn't the same as unknown. Every early copy that keeps a title gives the same four names. No early copy gives another.
If churches across the Roman world had guessed, you'd expect a Gospel of Andrew in one place and of Philip in another. We find none.
And look at two of the names. Mark and Luke weren't among the Twelve. Mark is remembered as the man who turned back partway through Paul's first mission.
When people did write gospels under famous names, they chose apostles, like Peter. Mark and Luke look less like a grab for authority than a memory nobody was free to improve.
Early in the second century, a writer named Papias passed on what an older teacher told him: that Mark had been Peter's interpreter, and wrote down what Peter remembered.
And Luke never claims to have seen Jesus. He says he carefully investigated what the eyewitnesses handed down. That's just what the church always said of him.
A skeptic can answer that witnesses alive somewhere don't help unless the writers used them. And memory is fragile.
That's fair. Memory bends, and a witness interprets as well as remembers.
But this story was told in churches where Peter, James and John had preached, among people who had heard them. It wasn't free to drift wherever anyone wished.
Some things stay open. Whether the apostle Matthew wrote the Gospel that bears his name, or stands behind it. Who the beloved disciple was. Exactly when Mark wrote.
Faithful Christians differ on those, and honest scholars live with them.
What the church confesses doesn't hang on a decade. It hangs on whether these books tell the truth about a man crucified under Pontius Pilate and raised on the third day.
And the earliest witness to that claim is older than any of the four.
You've probably heard this one. The emperor Constantine decided what went into the Bible, at the Council of Nicaea in 325.
He kept the books that suited the church in power, and buried the rest.
So what did Nicaea actually do?
The bishops answered Arius, who taught that the Son was a created being, and they wrote a creed against him.
They dealt with the date of Easter, a split in the church in Egypt, and twenty rules of church order.
Not one of their surviving decisions lists the books of Scripture.
Constantine did order fifty copies of the Scriptures for his new city. His letter names no books.
Here's the telling part. Eusebius, a bishop who was at Nicaea and admired Constantine, wrote a list of the New Testament books in those very years.
The four Gospels, Acts and Paul's letters were accepted everywhere. A few, like James, Jude and Second Peter, were still disputed. And he wasn't sure where to put Revelation.
If the emperor had settled it, his admirer had every reason to say so. He doesn't.
Go back further. In the 150s, Justin Martyr describes Christians on Sunday reading the memoirs of the apostles, which, he says, are called Gospels.
Around 180, Irenaeus says the Gospels can't be more or fewer than four.
That's a century and a half before Nicaea, while Christians were still a persecuted minority.
But weren't there other gospels? There were. Thomas, Peter, Mary, Judas.
Most scholars date them to the second century, after the four. None is earlier than the four on the usual dating, though some argue parts of Thomas carry older sayings.
Thomas is a collection of a hundred and fourteen sayings. It says nothing of Jesus' death and resurrection.
Around the year two hundred, a bishop named Serapion found a church reading a gospel under Peter's name.
At first he let them read it. Then he read it himself, found much in it sound and some things added, and judged it against what his churches had received.
That isn't a council imposing a list. It's a pastor reading a book and testing it.
One historian who studied all of this concluded, in effect, that no one chose the four Gospels. They were received.
The objection does get some things right. Early Christianity was varied. Paul himself wrote against people preaching another gospel.
The church did test books by their teaching, as well as by their link to the apostles and their use across the churches.
And the edges took centuries to settle. The first list that matches our twenty-seven books exactly comes from Athanasius, in 367. He was driven out of his city five times. He was no emperor's man.
Protestant, Catholic and Orthodox Bibles still differ in the Old Testament. But all of them share the same twenty-seven books of the New.
So the real question is which faith was there first.
The earliest Christian writings we have, Paul's letters from the fifties, already carry the faith of the four Gospels. Christ died for our sins, was buried, and was raised on the third day.
None of the gospels the church set aside is attested that early.
No emperor made the Bible. The churches received it, argued over its edges in the open, and said why.
You can read their reasons. Then read the books.
The Bible has been translated so many times. Hebrew to Greek, Greek to Latin, Latin to English. Like a photocopy of a photocopy.
Surely the meaning is lost by now.
But that isn't how any English Bible was made.
In 1526, William Tyndale translated the New Testament into English straight from the Greek. The King James translators of 1611 worked from the Hebrew and the Greek.
Modern Bibles translate from editions of the Hebrew and Greek built from the manuscripts.
So every translation goes back to the source. One English version's mistakes don't pass into the next. Each new translator starts again.
Still, something is always lost. The sound of a Hebrew psalm. A pun in Greek that isn't a pun in English.
Scholars who love the text say so. Robert Alter, who translated the Hebrew Bible himself, warns that modern versions too often explain where they should translate.
He's right that the temptation is real. Every reader should know that.
So why do English Bibles read differently?
Because translators choose. Some keep close to the shape of the original, its word order and its pictures. Others aim for plain, natural speech today.
Most Bibles sit somewhere between, and neither end is simply right.
Here's a place where it matters. In Romans, Paul writes a short Greek phrase that can mean faith in Christ, or the faithfulness of Christ.
Bibles differ on it, and scholars are divided. Good Bibles put the other reading in a note.
But either way, the gospel of the chapter stands. Righteousness comes from God, through Christ, to all who believe.
That's the pattern. The choices are fewer than the objection suggests, they're argued in the open, and the notes tell you where.
And what about verses that seem to be missing from newer Bibles?
The King James was translated from the printed Greek of its day, which rested on a small number of late copies.
Since then, thousands of manuscripts have been studied, many far older. In a few dozen places, they show words that copyists added over the centuries.
The differences run both ways. In Matthew, the oldest copies have Jesus say that not even the Son knows the day or the hour. The King James lacks those words. Modern Bibles put them back.
And the King James translators knew about variants too. In Luke, their own margin notes a verse missing from most Greek copies.
Here's something striking. The Gospels themselves are translations of a kind.
Jesus spoke Aramaic, and Mark keeps some of His words.
Taking her by the hand, Jesus said, “Talitha koum!” which means, “Little girl, I say to you, get up!”
Mark doesn't hide the translation. He shows it to you.
The faith has always moved by translation. A scholar raised a Muslim in the Gambia, Lamin Sanneh, argued that translatability became the way Christianity spread through history.
Today some part of the Bible exists in more than four thousand languages.
At Pentecost, the crowd asked:
How is it then that each of us hears them in his own native language?
So read more than one translation. Read the notes. Learn a little Greek or Hebrew if you can.
The meaning isn't lost. You're reading through a window someone else cleaned, and you can check the glass.
Does archaeology prove the Bible? Some say every dig confirms it.
Others say the spade has come up empty. No trace of the exodus, a Jericho without walls, little sign of Solomon's great kingdom.
The honest answer is neither.
Start with what didn't hold up.
For years, a shaft in Jerusalem was linked to the way David's men took the city. Later digging suggests it wasn't reachable in David's time.
Gates once credited to Solomon are now dated by some archaeologists to the century after him.
And for the exodus and the conquest, the ground is mostly silent.
But from the ninth century before Christ, Israel's neighbors and enemies start writing things down.
In 1993, at Tel Dan, diggers found pieces of an Aramaic victory stone. A king of Aram boasts of killing a king of the house of David.
Most scholars take it as the earliest known mention of David's dynasty by name, more than a century after him.
In 1868, in Moab, a black stone was found. King Mesha records how Omri, king of Israel, had oppressed his land, and how he broke free.
Second Kings tells it from Israel's side.
But after the death of Ahab, the king of Moab rebelled against the king of Israel.
The two accounts don't fit together in every detail. They agree on the main fact.
Then Assyria. Sennacherib invaded Judah, and the Bible says Hezekiah paid him thirty talents of gold.
Sennacherib's own annals boast that he shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem like a bird in a cage. They give the same thirty talents of gold. The silver differs.
And notice what the annals never claim. They never say the city was taken.
Hezekiah also cut a tunnel to bring water into the city.
It still runs under Jerusalem. An inscription found inside it in 1880 tells how the diggers, working toward each other, struck pick against pick, and the water flowed.
That's what independent sources look like. They agree on the main facts, differ in the details, and each tells the story from its own side.
Where the writers of Kings can be checked, they behave like historians of a kind.
But a stone can't show that God spoke to Moses. Inscriptions confirm names and events, not meanings.
And silence cuts both ways. It can't prove a great kingdom under Solomon, and it can't prove a small one.
Claims of proof and claims of disproof both say more than archaeology can.
The faith doesn't rest on a spade. It rests on what God did in history, above all the resurrection.
Archaeology shows the Old Testament's world was real. It was never going to be the ground of faith, and it hasn't taken it away.
Read the Gospels side by side, and you'll find places where they don't agree.
If the Bible can't keep its own story straight, why trust it?
Start here. These aren't modern discoveries. Christians noticed them from the start.
Early in the third century, Julius Africanus wrote about Jesus' two family trees. Around the year 400, Augustine wrote a whole book on how the Gospels agree.
The church never hid the hard places. It wrote about them.
Here's a real one. Matthew, Mark and Luke present the Last Supper as a Passover meal. John puts Jesus' trial on the day of Preparation, when the lambs were killed.
Careful scholars hold four different solutions, and each has a real weakness. The question isn't settled.
But look at what all four agree on. Jesus died under Pilate, in Jerusalem, at Passover, on a Friday, and was raised on the first day of the week.
Matthew and Luke give Jesus two different lists of ancestors between David and Joseph.
Some say Luke gives Mary's line. Others say one list is the royal line and the other the natural descent. Africanus offered his own answer and admitted he couldn't prove it.
No solution is established. But both lists make the same claim. Jesus, through Joseph, his legal father, was of the house of David. Paul had already said so in the fifties.
Luke ties Jesus' birth to a census under Quirinius. The historian Josephus dates that census about ten years after Herod died.
Several answers have been proposed, and none commands agreement. The question is open.
What it touches is the date of a census, not whether Jesus was born under Herod in David's town.
In the Old Testament, Kings and Chronicles tell the same reigns and sometimes give different numbers. Forty thousand stalls in one, four thousand in the other.
Many of these came from copying. Numbers were easy to miscopy, and some readings are impossible on the books' own figures.
And they show something else. The writer of Chronicles had the older books open in front of him, and he didn't hide them.
Here's the pattern. Independent accounts that agree at the center and differ at the edges are what historians usually find when a real event has been told more than once.
Differences at the edges don't turn the center into legend.
Christians also differ on how to say what this means. Some hold that Scripture is without error in all that it affirms.
Others hold it is infallible in what God gave it to teach, without requiring every number or date to be harmonized.
Both confess that God has spoken in Scripture, and that it is the church's final authority.
So read slowly. Put the accounts side by side. Notice the hard places.
You'll find that nearly every one sits at the edge of a story whose center they share.
Everything we meet came from something. You have parents. A tree came from a seed.
So here's a fair question, one children and philosophers both ask. If everything needs a cause, who made God?
Bertrand Russell gave it its plainest form, in a London lecture of 1927 published as Why I Am Not a Christian.
At eighteen he read John Stuart Mill's Autobiography. Mill's father had taught him that the question “Who made me?” can't be answered, because it raises another: “Who made God?”
Russell's conclusion: “If everything must have a cause, then God must have a cause. If there can be anything without a cause, it may just as well be the world as God.”
Richard Dawkins sharpened it in The God Delusion, in 2006: a God able to design a universe would have to be supremely complex, and so at least as improbable as the universe he's meant to explain.
Then God doesn't end the chain of questions. He starts a worse one.
A good deal of this is right. Christians have sometimes argued as if everything has a cause, and stated that way, the argument refutes itself.
And a designer pictured as a very complex being inside the universe, built from parts, would need explaining as much as anything he made.
Pause here and ask yourself: do the serious arguments really say everything has a cause? Or something narrower?
Something narrower. In William Lane Craig's form, the kalam argument says whatever begins to exist has a cause. It says nothing about what never began.
Leibniz in 1714, and Aquinas long before him, wrote about things that might not have existed. None of them says everything has a cause. Each says a certain kind of thing does.
So who made God is a fair question aimed at the wrong target. God, as Christians confess him, didn't begin, couldn't fail to be, and has no parts whose joining would need a cause.
Aquinas called God altogether simple, without parts. He isn't a very large thing inside the universe, needing a maker. He's the one on whom everything else depends.
Scripture speaks of God the same way.
Before the mountains were born or You brought forth the earth and the world, from everlasting to everlasting You are God.
Nothing made him, and nothing keeps him going.
The strongest reply is Russell's parity. You've granted that something exists without a cause outside itself. Then why not the universe, or its most basic laws?
It's a serious reply. Now the question isn't who made God, but which candidate can bear that weight.

The universe shows marks of something that might have been otherwise. Hume suggested it might be necessary in a way we don't understand. Observation can't rule that out, or rule out God. Argument has to decide.

Then the second half: isn't proof the believer's job? Russell imagined a china teapot circling the sun, too small for any telescope. No one could disprove it, and no one would be obliged to believe it.
Antony Flew argued in 1972 that the burden of proof lies on whoever affirms. He's partly right. Anyone who says God exists owes reasons.
Weigh this before the answer: what does the teapot explain? Nothing. Nothing would be different without it.

God is proposed to explain what everyone sees: a world that's ordered and knowable, and some things really wrong. The believer carries that burden. The unbeliever who says the universe needs no explanation carries one too.
Some things stay unresolved: whether a necessary being is a coherent idea, whether a necessary universe is a real alternative, and how to weigh either view before the evidence.

Christians differ too, on how to state God's simplicity; Alvin Plantinga questioned its strong form in 1980. What all confess is that God is uncreated and eternal, and that everything else exists because he wills it.
You created all things; by Your will they exist and came to be.
At the bush that burned and wasn't burned up, Moses asked God's name. The answer was “I AM WHO I AM.”
Every explanation has to stop somewhere. Ask yourself where yours stops, and why.
Does God actually exist? The case against is stronger than many believers admit, and nothing here forces anyone to agree.
But there are reasons, each open to inspection. This film weighs one: that anything exists at all.
In 1714 Gottfried Leibniz set down what he took to be the first question we have a right to ask.
“Why does something exist rather than nothing? For ‘nothing’ is simpler and easier than ‘something.’”
The universe, all of space, time, matter and energy, could have been different, or not been at all.
Pause here. In 1963 the philosopher Richard Taylor asked his readers to imagine finding a large translucent ball in the woods.
Would you think it simply exists, for no reason?
No one would. And making the ball the size of the universe doesn't make the question go away. It makes it bigger.
This argument doesn't need the universe to have had a beginning. Thomas Aquinas held that reason alone can't show the world began in time.
Alexander Pruss pictures an endless line of hens and eggs. Each hen is explained by an egg, each egg by a hen.
That still leaves untouched why there's such a line rather than none. A longer chain is still a chain that needs explaining.
One. Anything that exists but might not have existed has an explanation outside itself.
Two. The universe is that kind of thing.
Three. So its explanation is something that exists necessarily, not made of space, time or matter.
In David Hume's Dialogues, published in 1779 after his death, one speaker objects, “why may not the material universe be the necessarily existent Being”?
In 1948, debating the Jesuit Frederick Copleston on BBC radio, Bertrand Russell said, “I should say that the universe is just there, and that's all.”
To him, needing a cause for the whole because each part has one is like arguing that a wall must be small because each brick is.
Much of that is true. The principle that everything has an explanation can't be proved from anything more certain than itself.
In 2012 Lawrence Krauss argued that physical law can account for a universe coming to be without a creator.
And if the argument said everything needs a cause, God would need one too. That question has its own film.
A fair question before the answers: if every part of the universe might not have existed, what would make the whole unable not to exist?
Not every step from parts to whole is a mistake. A wall made entirely of brick is a brick wall.
And the nothing in Krauss's book, the philosopher David Albert objected, is a state described by quantum laws. That's still a universe that might not have been.
The strongest reply is parity. Every account of reality stops somewhere. The atheist may stop at the universe or its basic laws, and is no more irrational for doing so.

The answer is that the demand for a reason applies to what might not have been. Whether there can be a being whose existence isn't received from anything is the real crux, and philosophers divide over it.
Pause and ask yourself: where do you think explanations stop, and why?
If the argument is sound, it shows a necessary being that explains the universe. That's a large part of what believers in one God mean by the word.
It isn't proof in the mathematician's sense, and it isn't yet Christianity. It doesn't show that God is three persons, or that he became a man.
Paul in Athens began here.
The God who made the world and everything in it is the Lord of heaven and earth.
Then he went straight to the resurrection, a question of history.
Christians differ on how much this can carry. Some, following Aquinas, hold that reason can show God exists. Others hold that belief can be warranted without such arguments.
Russell's step is where an honest person can disagree. You can weigh all of this and still say no. What you can't honestly say is that there's nothing to weigh.
He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together.
If God is good, why is there so much suffering?
It's the strongest reason people give for not believing, and it deserves an honest answer, not a slogan.
It's old. Early in the fourth century a Christian teacher, Lactantius, preserved it to answer it, crediting it to Epicurus.
The suffering is real, and much of it looks pointless from where we stand.
Some answers Christians reach for first are worse than silence. Telling a grieving mother that everything happens for a reason isn't theology.
The Bible never pretends pain is good. At the grave of his friend Lazarus, Jesus wept.
Nobody can explain any one illness or disaster. When a tower fell in Siloam and eighteen people died, Jesus asked,
Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you.
He refused the old reading that people who suffer must be worse.
In 1955 the philosopher J. L. Mackie argued that three claims can't all be true together: God is all-powerful, God is wholly good, and evil exists.
Christians answer that evil comes from misused freedom. Mackie asked why God couldn't make people who are free and always choose the good.
Pause here and ask yourself. Could God make people truly free, and still guarantee that every one chooses well every time?
In 1974 Alvin Plantinga replied that a contradiction must be impossible, so a possible good reason is enough.
Creatures truly free to do right and wrong may be worth the risk.
Mackie later granted that evil doesn't show belief in God to be inconsistent, though he still asked whether that was a real solution.
It's a real result, and a narrow one. It explains no one's suffering, and many Reformed Christians reject its view of freedom. This film doesn't choose.
In 1979 the atheist philosopher William Rowe pictured a fawn caught in a forest fire no one sees, suffering that seems to serve no good.
We can see no reason for it, he said, so there probably is none. His argument hasn't been refuted.
Weigh it yourself. When you can't see a reason, how sure can you be that there isn't one?
In 1984 Stephen Wykstra asked when that step is fair. See no car in your garage, and there's none. See no flea across a room, and you can't be sure.
If God exists, the distance between his mind and ours is far greater.
In Job, the reader is shown a reason for Job's suffering, and Job is never told it. God answers him only with questions.
Rowe's reply is strong: a loving God would want to assure sufferers there is a reason, and many receive no such assurance.
Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth? Tell Me, if you have understanding.
Free will doesn't reach earthquakes, cancer or the suffering of animals. In 1989 Paul Draper argued that the pain in nature is what we'd expect if nothing behind it cared.
Christians give several answers, and differ over them: stable laws, long ages, a creation groaning until it's set free. Each has a cost.
But indifference has a cost too. It explains the pain well. It can't call it wrong, and it can't promise that it will end.
We know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until the present time.
What Christianity offers isn't an explanation but an event. God didn't stay outside the suffering.
The Son took a body that could be hurt, and on the cross he prayed the first line of Psalm 22.
My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?
If he was raised, then suffering is real evil, and it won't win. The risen Jesus still carried the marks of the nails.
No one can say why this child, why this disease, why this much. Job never found out. But he was allowed to ask, and at the end he said,
My ears had heard of You, but now my eyes have seen You.
The Bible's last picture is of God himself.
He will wipe away every tear from their eyes.
That doesn't tell anyone why. It tells us who has the last word, and that he has carried the wound himself.

films.title: Did Jesus really come back to life?

lines.text: Christians say God raised Jesus from the dead, in his body. It's fair to ask whether that happened.
History can't prove a miracle. But the case is stronger than most people have been told.
In 1748 David Hume argued that the dead staying dead is as uniform as experience gets. A witness to a rising is always more likely deceived or deceiving.
Bart Ehrman, an agnostic scholar, adds that the Gospels came decades later and that Rome often left the crucified unburied.
Grant what's true. Legends do grow. Grief does produce visions. A claim like this should face a higher bar.
Still, nearly every historian of the period, skeptics included, accepts a short list. First, Jesus was crucified under Pontius Pilate. Tacitus, a Roman historian who despised Christians, recorded it.
Second, his followers were soon convinced they'd seen him alive. Paul passes on a summary he received, which most scholars date within a few years.
E. P. Sanders, no apologist, judged their experiences a fact. What gave rise to them, he said, he did not know.
that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that He appeared to Cephas and then to the Twelve.
Third, two people with every reason not to believe came to believe. Paul had been trying to destroy the church. And James was Jesus' own brother.
For even His own brothers did not believe in Him.
Yet James went on to lead the church in Jerusalem until he was stoned around 62.
Pause here. What would it take to convince you your own brother had risen?
Fourth, the preaching began within weeks in Jerusalem, where he was buried and the claim was easiest to refute.
The empty tomb itself is more disputed. Historians still divide over it.
So weigh a fair question first. If you were inventing this story, who would bury Jesus, and who would find the tomb empty?
Mark names the man who buried him: Joseph of Arimathea, a prominent Council member. An inventor would more likely have picked a disciple.
All four Gospels put women first at the tomb, though Josephus summed up the law as, let not the testimony of women be admitted. That was for courts, so don't press it far.
The earliest opponents we know of never said the body was still there. They said it was stolen.
It was an argument among first-century Jews, Jesus' followers among them, over how the tomb became empty, not whether.
Their world had words for seeing the dead. When Peter, freed from prison, knocked at a gate, the believers inside said, It must be his angel.
Resurrection, N. T. Wright argues, meant something else: the bodily raising of God's people at the end of history. No one expected one man raised ahead of everyone while the world went on.
Each rival explains a part. Visions fit Peter's grief. But Paul wasn't mourning Jesus. He was hunting his followers.
Legend needs time, and the list came within a few years. Fraud means men suffered for the claim while knowing where they'd put the body.
And survival? David Friedrich Strauss, a skeptic, saw that a half-dead man needing bandages could never convince anyone he had conquered death.
The best reply mixes them: a lost grave, a vision, a conviction that spread, later legend. Any ordinary story, it says, beats a miracle.
But the pieces multiply, each thin where it most needs to be thick. And whether a natural story beats a miracle depends on whether there's a God who might raise the dead.
So ask yourself honestly. Had you already decided that God can't act, before you looked?
What exactly the witnesses saw is beyond the reach of history, and historians who grant their experiences disagree about the cause.
Christians differ on how much weight this kind of argument carries. Together they confess that the body that was buried was raised.
History won't carry anyone to faith. It can move a person from dismissing the claim to weighing it. Matthew doesn't hide the doubt.
When they saw Him, they worshiped Him, but some doubted.
You can weigh it all and still say no. Just don't say no without the weighing.
An open Bible on one side of the table. A small telescope on the other.
Plenty of people say they're enemies, and that you'll have to pick one.
Pause and ask yourself where you first heard that. Then let's test it.
The war picture came from John William Draper in 1874, and Andrew Dickson White, the first president of Cornell, in 1896.
They gave the modern world two forces, one marching toward the light and the other holding it back. At the center stands Galileo.
The core is true. In 1616 Rome's theologians judged the sun-centered view formally heretical.
In 1633 the Roman Inquisition declared Galileo vehemently suspected of heresy. He was made to renounce his view on his knees, and he lived under house arrest until he died.
The church was wrong, and Christians should say so plainly.
Galileo was a believer. He quoted Augustine: for an unbeliever to hear a Christian talk nonsense about the natural world was a disgraceful and dangerous thing.
And the earth's motion hadn't been proved. Friedrich Bessel first measured its decisive sign in 1838.
When James Clerk Maxwell's Cavendish Laboratory opened at Cambridge in the 1870s, its doors carried a Psalm in Latin.
Great are the works of the LORD; they are pondered by all who delight in them.
Gregor Mendel, whose peas began genetics, was a friar. In 1927 Georges Lemaître, a Catholic priest, argued that the universe is expanding.
None of that proves Christianity. Plenty of great scientists have been unbelievers. It shows the war is a story about science, not a finding of it.
The strong objection is quieter. Science keeps explaining what God was once used to explain. In 1859 Darwin gave a natural account of how living things fit their lives.
The biologist Jerry Coyne adds that science can find out it's wrong, and religion can't.
A fair question before the answer comes: if every gap closes, is anything left for God?
Christians have often put God in the gaps. In 1944 Dietrich Bonhoeffer warned against it: We are to find God in what we know, not in what we don't know.
Thomas Aquinas taught that God works through the causes he made, not in competition with them. An author is the cause of every line in a novel without being one of its characters.
He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together.
Water boils because the molecules are agitated. The kettle is on because someone wanted tea. Both answers are true, and they don't compete.
If God isn't found in the gaps, Christians can't argue for him from the gaps either.
The physicist Eugene Wigner, in 1960, called the power of mathematics to describe the world a wonderful gift which we neither understand nor deserve. Science rests on something it doesn't explain.
Christians also argue over Genesis 1, and it isn't new. In the third century Origen asked how there were days before the sun. In the fourth, Basil said, For me grass is grass.
Today some read six ordinary days, not long ago. Some read long ages. Some read a literary frame, God's workweek, or a cosmic temple. Some hold that God created through evolution.
Each is held by believers who take Scripture seriously, and each has a hard question. This film takes no side. Which had you assumed was the only Christian view?
In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.
Every reading confesses that God made everything, by his word, that it was good, and that we bear his image.
The Apostles' Creed confesses the Maker of heaven and earth. It says nothing of how long the making took.
