None of this proves God exists or settles the age of the earth. It clears away a false choice.
It is the glory of God to conceal a matter and the glory of kings to search it out.
Science is that searching, and Christians have every reason to love it. Science hands us a magnificent description of the house. It can't tell us whether anyone lives there.
If God is real, why can't anyone see him? It's a fair question, and the Bible doesn't dodge it.
Jesus said it plainly: God is Spirit. He isn't made of anything, because nothing made him.
That alone doesn't make him unreal. We know real things we can't see all the time, like love, the wind, our own thoughts.
Pause here and ask yourself: how do you know the wind is there? No one has ever seen it. Everyone has seen a tree bend in it.
Christians call this general revelation: what God shows of himself to every person through the created world.
The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of His hands.
But the sky can't say everything. General revelation leaves every person accountable; special revelation tells the good news.
So God spoke, to Abraham, to Moses, through the prophets, and their words were written down.
At Sinai, Moses reminded Israel, “You heard the sound of the words, but saw no form; there was only a voice.”
In 1993 the philosopher J. L. Schellenberg made the argument that has shaped the debate since, in a book called Divine Hiddenness and Human Reason.
Some people are open to God, yet through no fault of their own they don't believe he exists. A perfectly loving God would never leave such a person without the evidence. So there's no such God.
His point isn't that God is unproved. It's that the silence itself is evidence. A loving parent doesn't hide from a child who's calling for her.
There are honest unbelievers. Many have prayed, read, asked and waited for years, and haven't come to believe.
Christians have sometimes read Paul in Romans as a verdict on every doubter. Paul was describing the human race, not reading the heart of the person across the table.
Scripture itself knows the ache. Isaiah says, “Truly You are a God who hides Himself.”

Blaise Pascal saw it three centuries earlier. In his Pensées, published in 1670, he wrote, “There is enough light for those who only desire to see, and enough obscurity for those who have a contrary disposition.”
Weigh this: if God were as plain as the sun, could anyone still come to him freely?
Michael Murray argued in 1993 that overwhelming evidence would coerce the response it meant to invite. John Hick had argued in 1966 that an obvious God would leave no room to grow freely toward him.
Schellenberg's reply is strong. Freedom, humility, growth: every one could be had inside a relationship with God, and better there. And what of a child who never resisted anything?
It isn't fully answered. Christians reply in part that believing God exists is the door, not the room. A person can hold the belief and refuse the relationship.
anyone who approaches Him must believe that He exists and that He rewards those who earnestly seek Him
And Christians claim God didn't stay hidden. He came near, in a way that could be missed.
No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father’s side, has made Him known.

Jesus told Philip, “Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father,” and was crucified by people who didn't see it. In 1518 Martin Luther spoke of the theologian of the cross, who knows God hidden in suffering and the cross.
Some things stay unresolved. Why some who seek don't find, or find only late, isn't explained. No one can see into another's heart.

Christians differ. Many in the Reformed tradition read Romans 1 to say no unbelief is wholly innocent, though no one may judge another's heart. Others hold that some sincere seekers haven't yet found.
Scripture calls the seeking long, and the finding promised: “You will seek Me and find Me when you search for Me with all your heart.”
Christian hope ends where this question begins. Paul says, “Now we see but a dim reflection as in a mirror; then we shall see face to face.”
And Jesus left a word for everyone who has never seen him: “blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.”

films.title: Why does God seem silent sometimes?

lines.text: You pray, and nothing happens. No answer, no sign, only quiet.
Another film asks why we can't see God at all. This one is closer to home: the God you trust seems to have gone quiet.
Start with one sentence worth holding on to. Feeling far from God is not the same as being far from him.
The Bible doesn't hide this. In Psalm 13, David asks God the same question four times.
How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever? How long will You hide Your face from me?
In Israel, God's face meant his favor and presence. And to be forgotten by God meant to be left without help.
David wasn't doubting that God was there. He was protesting an absence he felt. The lament was an act of faith, not its collapse.
Since Hermann Gunkel, scholars have traced the shape of such prayers: complaint, petition, then trust and a promise to praise.
In Psalm 13 each part is shorter than the one before. The turn comes on one small word in verse five: But.
And nothing has changed. No rescue is reported. David trusts in the dark, leaning on God's loyal love, the Hebrew word chesed.
But I have trusted in Your loving devotion; my heart will rejoice in Your salvation.
Pause here and ask yourself. Does that turn feel too quick, even forced?
Readers have asked the same. Some think a priest or prophet spoke a word of assurance. Others think the change happened inside the one praying.
Others say the psalm compresses what may take a long time, a prayer prayed many times before the ending feels true.
Whichever is right, the complaint stays in the psalm. Trust is spoken beside it, not in place of it.
Elijah had just seen fire fall on Mount Carmel. Then one threat came from Jezebel, and he ran for his life into the wilderness.
Exhausted and afraid, he sat under a broom tree and told God, I have had enough, LORD.
The Bible doesn't criticize that prayer or hide it. And look at the order of God's answer: sleep, food, water, and a second meal, before any words at all.
Then he lay down under the broom tree and fell asleep.
Then at Horeb, the mountain of God, a great wind tore at the rocks. Then an earthquake, then a fire. God was in none of them.
And after the fire came a still, small voice.
The Hebrew is a paradox, literally a voice of thin silence. Translations differ: a gentle whisper, a sound of sheer silence.
God asked Elijah a question, gave him work, and told him he wasn't alone: seven thousand were still faithful.
The church has named this for centuries. The sixteenth-century Spanish mystic John of the Cross called it the dark night of the soul.
He treated the felt absence as a stage of love being purified, not as a punishment.
Mother Teresa, who served the dying in Calcutta, lived decades in this dryness and kept serving anyway.
Weigh this. If people like that felt it for years, what does your own quiet prove about you?
On the cross, Jesus prayed the first line of Psalm 22, Israel's fullest prayer for the moment when God seems gone.
My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?
The Son of God took that cry onto his own lips. And Psalm 22, at its lowest point, breaks off to declare that God has answered.
That afternoon wasn't the end. On the third day he was raised.
No one can promise when the quiet will lift. The psalm gives no date for the morning.
So don't measure God's nearness by your feelings. They rise and fall with sleep, grief and the weather.
Keep the practices when the warmth is gone. Tell one honest believer where you are.
And read the psalms of absence. They were written by people who felt exactly this and were not cast off.
The LORD is near to the brokenhearted; He saves the contrite in spirit.
Psalm 13 ends with a promise to sing, and a verb in the past tense.
I will sing to the LORD, for He has been good to me.
The complaint is still there. So is the trust. Both are prayer.
What happens when we die?
Most people ask it first when death comes close to someone they love, and it can be hard to say out loud.
The Bible doesn't tell us everything. It tells us enough to hope.
The Bible never pretends death isn't real. Dust returns to dust.
The Old Testament speaks of Sheol, the realm of the dead, about sixty-five times, and several psalms ask who can praise God from there. It doesn't rush to comfort.
Yet one psalm says to God, if I make my bed in Sheol, You are there.
Jesus stood at his friend Lazarus' grave and wept. Grief is not unbelief.
Paul never told grieving Christians to stop being sad. He wrote,
We do not want you to be uninformed about those who sleep in death, so that you will not grieve like the rest, who are without hope.
Some people revived after their hearts stopped report leaving their bodies, a light, and meeting relatives who had died.
Since Raymond Moody's Life After Life in 1975, many studies have followed.
In 1998 J. P. Moreland and Gary Habermas argued the best cases show a person can survive the body.
Pause here and ask yourself. If someone came back and told you what they saw, would that settle it?
The experiences are real, and the people who have them aren't lying or foolish.
But in 1987 Carol Zaleski showed that the accounts vary with what each culture expects, and similar experiences come to people who only believed they were dying.
The Stanford Encyclopedia's entry on the afterlife says we may be close to an impasse. Christians differ over these experiences, and this film doesn't choose.
Christian hope never rested on them. It rests on something of another kind.
Not that someone near death saw a light, but that a man who was certainly dead, executed by Rome, didn't stay dead.
A skeptic will say Easter is the same kind of story, told long ago. Fair. But the earliest summary, which Paul passed on, names events, not visions: died, buried, raised, appeared.
Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.
So what happens between a believer's death and the resurrection? Theologians call it the intermediate state.
Paul calls death sleep. Yet Jesus told the criminal beside him, today you will be with Me in Paradise, and Paul wrote,
I desire to depart and be with Christ, which is far better indeed.
Most Protestant churches, with the Heidelberg Catechism and the Westminster Confession, hold that believers go at once to be with Christ, at rest, while the body waits.
The Catholic Church teaches purgatory, a purification after death, which its defenders call a work of grace. The Orthodox pray for the departed. The Reformers rejected purgatory.
Others, among them John Milton and the Seventh-day Adventist Church, hold that the dead sleep, and their next waking moment is the resurrection.
Weigh it yourself. Paul calls death both sleep and being with Christ. What does each picture protect?
Here they all agree. The dead in Christ are waiting for the same morning. The resurrection, not the time between, is the final hope.
Around 160 Justin Martyr warned against those who denied the resurrection and said souls simply go up to heaven at death.
Our word cemetery comes from a Greek word for a sleeping place. The first Christians expected those laid there to wake.
God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep in Him.
Grief is not faithlessness, because the separation is real. Comfort is not denial. God holds both sides of death.
Ask yourself. What would it look like to be truly sad and truly hopeful at the same time?
On the night before he died, Jesus comforted his frightened friends with a promise of a place.
The rooms in his Father's house mean belonging and presence. The goal is to be where Jesus is.
I will come back and welcome you into My presence, so that you also may be where I am.

films.title: What about people who never heard?

lines.text: Picture a woman who lived a thousand years ago, in a village where the name of Jesus had never been spoken.
She was honest. She loved her children. She prayed to whatever she knew of God. What becomes of her?
Kenneth Himma made her into an argument in 2002. A perfectly good God wouldn't punish people who aren't to blame, and people of other faiths generally aren't to blame for their beliefs.
John Hick added the fact underneath. In God Has Many Names, in 1980, he wrote that a person's religion depends, in the great majority of cases, on where he was born. Is salvation, then, luck?
Much of this is true, and Scripture said it first. Abraham pressed God: Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right? God didn't rebuke the question. He answered it.
And most people who have ever lived never heard the name of Jesus. A shrug is the wrong answer.
Pause here and ask yourself: is saved only by Christ the same claim as saved only by knowing his name in this life?
The objection runs them together. Scripture keeps them apart. The church confesses the first without hedging: there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved.
Peter said that as a prisoner on trial. It wasn't a boast. The second claim may be true. But it's a different claim.
Abraham lived long before Bethlehem, yet Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness.
Every Christian tradition holds that he was saved by Christ, by a work done centuries later.
Scripture measures judgment by the light a person had. No one in it is condemned for never hearing a name.
But Paul also says all have sinned. So weigh this: can someone be rescued by a Christ he never knew? Faithful Christians answer that in more than one way.
the work of the law is written on their hearts
The first answer is often called restrictivism. A person must hear the gospel and trust Christ in this life. Ronald Nash argued for it in 1994.
No one is condemned for not hearing, its holders add, only for sin against the light he had, and God may bring the gospel to anyone who seeks him.
Its hardest question: the multitudes who lived and died with no messenger in reach.
And how can they believe in the One of whom they have not heard?
The second is often called inclusivism. No one is saved apart from Christ, but his work may reach some who never knew his name and who answered, in faith, the light God gave them.
Karl Rahner is its best-known defender. Clark Pinnock argued a form of it in 1992.
Its hardest question: why does the New Testament press so hard on hearing? Even devout Cornelius still had to be told.

A third answer: everyone will meet Christ and be able to answer him, at death or after it. Its holders read Peter's words, the gospel was preached even to those who are now dead, as a door the church shouldn't close.
Its hardest question: man is appointed to die once, and after that to face judgment.
Some, like Origen and Gregory of Nyssa, have hoped God will in the end restore all. The church's councils and confessions have generally not received that hope.
The strongest reply: this is a distinction without comfort. If only those who hear can be rescued, rescue still depends on where you were born.

That's fair, and it lands on one Christian view, not on the confession. Inclusivists deny its premise. Some restrictivists argue that God, knowing what every person would freely do, may leave no one who would have believed without the chance; critics answer that this can't be shown true. Others confess that his ways are above ours. A viewer may find none of these sufficient.
Which answer is right, the creeds don't settle, and this film won't either.
What all confess is who the Judge is. The Father judges no one, but has assigned all judgment to the Son, the one who wept at a friend's grave.
Almost everyone who asks this has heard. Pause and ask yourself what you're meant to do with what you've been told.

films.title: Why are there so many churches?

lines.text: Read the church signs in one town: Catholic, Orthodox, Baptist, Methodist, Pentecostal. A fair question: if there's one Lord, why so many churches?
It began as one company in Jerusalem, gathered by the Spirit at Pentecost.
They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and to the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer.
From Jerusalem the message went to Samaria, to Antioch, where the disciples were first called Christians, and on to Rome.
Worship took different shapes in different languages, but the churches confessed one faith, later written in the creeds.
Over centuries, the church drifted. The East spoke Greek, the West Latin, and in time most on each side couldn't read the other's books.
When the western empire fell, the West looked to the bishop of Rome. The East still had its emperor.
Pause here and ask yourself: when the whole church must decide something, who has the last word?
The West increasingly said Rome, Peter's successor. The East honored Rome as first among the great churches, but held that the bishops govern together, in council.
Then one Latin word, filioque, “and the Son,” added to the creed in the West: the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.
The West meant to guard the Son's full divinity. The East objected to the words, and to one region changing the whole church's creed. The history course says neither was simply wrong.
In 1054, at Hagia Sophia, Cardinal Humbert excommunicated the patriarch Michael Cerularius, who returned the favor.
That only made visible a split already real. It was sealed in 1204, when a Western crusading army sacked Constantinople.

In 1965 the pope and the patriarch lifted the old excommunications. The course finds no hero and no villain, “only two faithful traditions that loved the same Lord and lost the ability to love each other.”
A German monk, Martin Luther, found peace with God in Paul's letter to the Romans: the righteousness God requires is the righteousness God gives, received by faith.
In 1517 he posted ninety-five theses against the sale of indulgences. He meant to start a debate. The printing press made it a fire across Europe.
For the gospel reveals the righteousness of God that comes by faith from start to finish

The movement grew beyond him: Zwingli in Zurich, who broke with Luther over the Supper; Calvin in Geneva; the Anabaptists, who baptized only those who could profess faith; and in England, the Anglican tradition.
Protestants divided further, Baptist, Methodist, Pentecostal and more, often over baptism, the Supper, and who holds authority and how.
Rome didn't stand still. The Council of Trent, from 1545 to 1563, drew clear lines: justification by grace, but not by faith alone.
It also cleaned house: a seminary for every diocese. The Jesuits arose, and saints like Teresa of Avila. Rome did reform, and the reform was real.
The tearing was soaked in blood. Catholics killed Protestants, Protestants killed Catholics, and both killed the Anabaptists.
The wars of religion ended in exhaustion, with the Peace of Westphalia in 1648. Nobody had won.
Some divisions were over things that matter. Some were not worth what they cost. The church needed the recovery, and the church should mourn the blood.
Weigh this: which differences are worth disagreeing over, and which aren't?

Some are real. Catholics confess one visible church centered on Peter's successor; the Orthodox, a communion of churches whose bishops are equals; many Protestants, a church known where the gospel is rightly preached; free churches, a gathered company of believers.
And under them all: “Most of these churches confess the same God, the same Christ, the same empty tomb, and they recite the same ancient creeds.”
Why not skip them all? The New Testament has no word for a Christian who belongs to no church. Paul's picture is a body, and a hand on its own isn't freer. It's dying.
The night before he died, Jesus prayed for all who would believe:
That all of them may be one, as You, Father, are in Me, and I am in You.
The divisions are real. So is the unity under them. This film doesn't choose between the churches.
Christians say God became a man. So which was Jesus?
God only wearing a body? Or a good man later called God?
The church's answer is neither.
It's called the incarnation, from the Latin word for flesh.
The eternal Son of God, without ceasing to be God, became a man, Jesus of Nazareth, conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the virgin Mary.
He took a whole human nature, body and soul, mind and will.
One person, fully God and fully man.
The Old Testament doesn't say this outright. But it builds a longing.
At Sinai, Israel heard a voice but saw no form.
Yet God had His people build a tent so He could dwell among them. And His glory filled it.
Later, Solomon dedicated the temple and asked if God would really dwell on earth.
The promises of a coming king lean the same way.
Isaiah spoke of a son called Immanuel, God with us. Two chapters later, a child from David's house is called Mighty God.
And Malachi said the Lord would suddenly come to His temple.
Then John says it plainly.
The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us. We have seen His glory, the glory of the one and only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth.
In Greek, made His dwelling means pitched His tent, the same word used for the tabernacle.
The glory that filled that tent is now seen in a man.
The Gospels show a real human life. He grows, and He gets hungry.
He sleeps in a boat. He weeps at a friend's tomb.
In Gethsemane He's deeply troubled, and yields His will to the Father's.
Yet He forgives sins, which only God can do. He commands the sea, and it obeys.
No wonder the disciples asked who this could be.
The early church guarded both sides.
Around the year 110, Ignatius of Antioch answered those who said Christ only seemed to have a body. He was truly born, Ignatius wrote, and truly suffered and died.
When a teacher denied Christ a human mind, Gregory of Nazianzus answered that what Christ did not take on, He did not heal.
In 451, the Council of Chalcedon set the boundaries. One person in two natures, neither mixed nor changed, neither divided nor separated.
Christians who confess all this still differ on some questions.
Would the Son have come if we had never sinned? Thomas Aquinas judged it more fitting to say no, since Scripture gives the remedy for sin as the reason.
John Duns Scotus said yes, because Christ was the goal of creation from the start.
And when Paul says Christ emptied Himself, did He veil His glory, or lay aside the use of some divine powers for a time? Christians answer both ways.
When Christians ask what God is like, they look at Jesus.
He spent most of His years in a small town, working with His hands. Nothing human is beneath God's notice.
And the One Christians pray to has been where they are.
For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but we have one who was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin.
He still bears a human nature in heaven. The hope isn't escape from being human, but renewal, soul and body.
He was rich and became poor for others, and Paul makes that the pattern for how Christians treat each other.
God isn't a distant idea. He has a face and a name, and pitched His tent among us.
It's the oldest question in religion. How can a person be in the right with God?
Job asked it. So has anyone who felt they didn't measure up.
The Bible answers with a word from the courtroom. Justify.
To justify is what a judge does when he rules that someone stands in the right.
But God will not acquit the guilty. And the Psalms admit no one alive is righteous before Him.
So how can a just judge rule for the guilty?
The first hint of an answer comes under a night sky.
God shows Abram the stars and promises children beyond counting. Abram is old and childless.
Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness.
That's centuries before the law. Paul reads it as God counting a man righteous whose only part was trust in a promise.
Jesus told of a tax collector who only asked for mercy. He went home justified, and the Pharisee did not.
Paul says sinners are justified freely, by God's grace, through what Christ has done.
The cross is how God stays just while putting the ungodly in the right. Their sin is dealt with, not waved away.
The gift is received through faith, not earned by keeping the law.
But James writes that a person is justified by deeds, and not by faith alone.
Most interpreters say Paul asks how a sinner is accepted, while James attacks a faith that does nothing.
Others think James means the final verdict. Either way, the faith that receives the gift is never alone.
The earliest Christian writers repeated Paul's words without a quarrel.
Augustine taught that justification is wholly God's gracious act, and took the Latin word to mean making righteous.
With Martin Luther, the Reformation made it a dividing question. The Catholic Church answered at the Council of Trent, in 1547.
Christians differ here.
Lutheran and Reformed Christians teach that justification is a verdict. God forgives the sinner and credits to him Christ's righteousness.
Faith is the empty hand that receives it. A changed life always follows, but it's never the ground of the verdict.
Catholics teach that God doesn't only forgive. He truly makes the sinner righteous, pouring His love into the heart by the Holy Spirit.
Grace comes first, and no one can earn it. Faith is the root, joined with hope and love.
Because it's a real change, it can grow, be lost through grave sin, and be restored through repentance and the sacrament of penance.
The Orthodox confess salvation as entirely God's gift in Christ, but their main picture is theosis, union with God, not a courtroom.
They generally see the Western quarrel as resting on a line between declaring and making righteous that they never drew.
All of them reject the idea of standing before God on your own record, apart from grace.

In 1999, the Lutheran World Federation and the Catholic Church signed a joint declaration of shared basic truths, leaving real differences open. Many confessional Lutherans, Reformed and evangelicals judged it papered over them.
Someone who keeps their own accounts with God is never at rest. The books never balance.
Being justified brings peace with God. Someone who knows they're accepted can afford to tell the truth about their sin.
The tax collector and the Pharisee, the churchgoer and the latecomer, stand on the same footing.
The acquitted have every reason to pass that mercy on.
Therefore, there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
No one can put themselves in the right with God. It's His work, and it comes as a gift.
Read the New Testament and you keep running into a small phrase. In Christ.
What does that mean? How can one person be in another?
A Christian isn't only helped by Jesus from a distance. A Christian is joined to him.
What's true of him becomes true of them. They died with him, were raised with him, and will appear with him.
The Holy Spirit makes that bond, and faith receives it.
Paul uses it, and close cousins like in him, all through his letters. In 1892 the scholar Adolf Deissmann counted a hundred and sixty-four of them.
He also reaches for words that mean with. Crucified with. Buried with. Raised with.
The Old Testament never says this outright. It gives the ground the idea grows from.
A God who makes his home in the middle of his people.
A Hebrew word for clinging, used when husband and wife become one flesh. The prophets made that bond a picture of God's love.
And one standing for many, the way Adam's choice reached the whole human race.
Israel had been God's vine. Jesus took the picture for himself.
I am the vine and you are the branches. The one who remains in Me, and I in him, will bear much fruit. For apart from Me you can do nothing.
Belonging to God's people now means being a branch in him.
Later the risen Jesus asked Saul, who was persecuting the church, why Saul was persecuting him.
To strike the church is to strike Christ.
For Paul, Adam and Christ each stand for a whole humanity. Joined to Adam, people share his death. Joined to Christ, they share his life.
Believers were buried with him through baptism, so they could walk in a new life.
Every spiritual blessing is given in him. Chosen in him. Redeemed in him. Sealed with the Spirit in him.
And no one is joined to him alone. Together, believers are his body.
Around the year 180, Irenaeus taught that Jesus went back over the ground where Adam failed, obeying where Adam disobeyed, so those joined to him share his victory.
In his Institutes, John Calvin wrote that as long as Christ stays outside us, all he suffered and did is no use to us.
The Holy Spirit, he said, is the bond that joins us to him.
Christians describe this union in different ways.
Reformed Christians say believers receive two gifts in him, never separated. Declared right with God, and made new.
Lutherans say Christ comes through Word and sacrament. Luther pictured a joyful exchange. Christ takes the believer's sins and gives his righteousness.
Roman Catholics say baptism joins a person to Christ and his body, the church, and the Eucharist feeds that union.
The Orthodox call it theosis, sharing by grace in God's life, while God's essence stays beyond every creature.
Every one of them insists it's by grace. A creature joined to God is still a creature.
This changes where a Christian finds who they are.
For you died, and your life is now hidden with Christ in God.
Failure and success are real. But they don't define someone whose life is found in another.
Suffering isn't proof that God is absent. It can be one of the ways the union is lived.
And the people beside them at the Lord's Supper, however different, belong to the same body.
Even death doesn't break it. Paul calls believers who have died the dead in Christ, still in him, waiting for the resurrection.
No part of a Christian's life, not even its end, is outside of Christ.
You've trusted Christ, and you know you're forgiven. So why are you still fighting the same old sins?
And if God already accepts you, does it matter how you live?
The Bible answers both with one word. Sanctification.
To be holy is first to belong to God, set apart for him, and then to become like him.
Sanctification is the Holy Spirit's lifelong work of setting believers apart and making them like Jesus Christ.
It isn't justification, God's verdict that you're in the right, but the two never come apart.
Scripture speaks in two tenses. Believers already are sanctified, and they're being sanctified.
Paul wrote to a church full of factions and lawsuits, and still told them they'd been sanctified.
A saint, in the Bible, isn't a rare hero. It's any member of God's people.
One tense is still to come. When Christ appears, his people will be like him.
Holiness starts as God's claim. At Sinai he claims a whole people, holy because he chose them.
Leviticus calls Israel to be holy as God is holy, then to leave the edges of the harvest for the poor.
Holiness meant being like a God who cares for the poor.
Through Ezekiel, God promised his people a new heart, and his Spirit within them.
The night before he died, Jesus prayed for his disciples to be sanctified, and set himself apart for their sake.
Hebrews says believers were sanctified once for all by his sacrifice, and are still being sanctified.
Is grace a license to sin? No, says Paul, because believers have died with Christ and been set free from sin.
So who does the work, God or you? Paul says both.
Continue to work out your salvation, he writes. Then he says why.
For it is God who works in you to will and to act on behalf of His good purpose.
And the Spirit grows one fruit, not many. Love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control.
In the late fourth century, Gregory of Nyssa called perfection endless growth into God, because God has no end.
Augustine taught that holiness itself is a gift of grace, and that no one in this life is without sin.
Christians differ on how far holiness reaches in this life.
Reformed churches teach a decisive break with sin's rule, then slow growth, never finished in this life.
Lutherans stress living from forgiveness, a daily return to baptism, and not trusting your own progress.
Wesleyan and Holiness churches teach entire sanctification, a heart so full of love that the will is wholly God's, though not sinless perfection.
Keswick teaching calls for a decisive act of surrender and faith, then a life of consistent victory.
Catholics speak of grace growing through the sacraments, the Orthodox of theosis, lifelong growth into likeness to God.
So because you're already set apart and loved, failure doesn't undo your standing.
And because God means to make you like Christ, you can't make peace with your sin either.
The means are ordinary: Scripture, prayer, confession, the Lord's Supper, other believers, small duties, even hardship.
Growth is often slow, and others tend to see it before you do.
Zechariah saw a day when every cooking pot in Jerusalem would be holy.
Holiness reaches into how you pay a worker, treat the disabled, talk about people and forgive.
It all rests on a promise. The God who began the work will finish it.
The One who calls you is faithful, and He will do it.
Christians press on, not to earn the day Christ appears, but because it's coming.

films.title: Does God still love me when I do wrong?

lines.text: You did something wrong, and a heavy question follows: has God turned away from me?
Religious leaders once grumbled that Jesus welcomed sinners and ate with them.
He answered with three stories of something lost and found. Luke calls them one parable. The last is about a father and two sons.
This man welcomes sinners and eats with them.
The younger son asks for his share of the estate while his father is still alive. That was unusual.
He turns family land into cash, leaves for a distant country, and wastes it all. The Greek word means wastefully, recklessly. That's what prodigal means.
Nothing in the story pretends this was small.
Then famine. Feeding pigs for a Gentile and envying their food was the lowest point imaginable for a Jewish son.
He came to his senses and rehearsed a speech. Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. Then a request to be hired as a servant.
Readers differ on that speech. It echoes Pharaoh's words to Moses, so some hear a bargain. Others hear the Bible's ordinary form of confession.
So he got up and went to his father. But while he was still in the distance, his father saw him and was filled with compassion. He ran to his son, embraced him, and kissed him.
The father's love is moved before any confession.
Kenneth Bailey argued that an old landowner running in public was shameful. Critics reply that the evidence for that is late. Either way, he ran.
The son starts his speech. The father never lets him reach the part about being a servant. Robe, ring and sandals answer it instead.
Pause here and ask yourself. What speech have you rehearsed for God? This son was embraced before he said a word of his.
For this son of mine was dead and is alive again! He was lost and is found!
Does that make wrong small? No. Repentance is the human side of being found by God. The father's welcome runs ahead of it. It doesn't cancel it.
In 1937 Dietrich Bonhoeffer called forgiveness without repentance cheap grace.
And real love corrects. Love isn't measured by what it permits, but by what it gives.
For the Lord disciplines the one He loves
Weigh a fair objection. The father forgives with no sacrifice and no payment. So is the cross unnecessary?
Faustus Socinus argued that God, like a creditor, can simply cancel a debt. Jewish readers add that God has always received the one who returns. There's truth in that.
But a parable makes a few points, not every point. Paul names the cost. God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Some people believe all this and still keep their own accounts. The books never balance.
Repentance isn't self-punishment. You don't have to feel sorry enough before God will listen. It's turning around and going home.
If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins.
The older son never left, yet he refuses to come in. He counts his years at home like wages.
So the father goes out to him too. Son, you are always with me, he says.
Most commentators, Christian and Jewish, read him as a warning to religious people of every kind, Christians included, who resent mercy shown to others.
The story ends with him outside, deciding. Pause here and ask yourself which son you're more like today.
and all that is mine is yours
Many find it easier to serve God than to believe he delights in them. But he set his love on his people because he loved them.
If your own father was absent or cruel, that picture may be hard. Jesus told the same love as a shepherd, and a woman sweeping her house.
And nothing in all creation can separate his people from it.
nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

films.title: Why did God let his temple be destroyed?

lines.text: In 587 or 586 BC, Babylon's army burned the temple in Jerusalem. Historians give either year.
It was Solomon's temple, where God's Name dwelt.
Why would God let his own house be destroyed?
Solomon had given part of the answer on the day it was finished. Even heaven, the highest heaven, cannot contain You, much less this temple I have built.
The temple was never a box that held God.
For more than three centuries God sent prophets: Elijah, Amos, Hosea, Isaiah, Micah, Jeremiah and others.
Chronicles gives the reason. Again and again the LORD, the God of their fathers, sent word to His people through His messengers because He had compassion on them.
Every warning was an act of mercy.
About 609 BC, God sent Jeremiah to the temple gate, the most public pulpit in Judah.
Since God had saved Jerusalem from Sennacherib in 701 BC, many decided he would never let his house fall.
So Jeremiah warned them. Do not trust in deceptive words, chanting: ‘This is the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD.’
The sermon nearly cost him his life.
Pause here and ask yourself. What's the difference between trusting a place and trusting God?
Ezekiel, already an exile, saw in a vision that the glory of the LORD left the temple before the city fell.
The exile was not God losing a battle to Babylon's gods. It was God doing what he had said he would do.
Then the glory of the LORD moved away from the threshold of the temple
After a siege of about a year and a half, the temple, the palace and the city were burned, and many survivors were carried off to Babylon.
The Chronicler doesn't linger on the details. He gives the reason: God's messengers were mocked until there was no remedy.
He burned down the house of the LORD
The Bible doesn't treat the grief as small.
By the rivers of Babylon we sat and wept when we remembered Zion.
They hung their harps on the willows. How can we sing a song of the LORD in a foreign land?
The psalm ends with a raw cry for justice. It's a prayer, not a command, and it hands that demand to God.
Lamentations gives five poems to the same loss, four of them running through the Hebrew alphabet, grief from A to Z.
Now weigh the hardest question fairly. Can suffering this great ever be proportionate?
Lamentations asks that, and leaves the question before God.
The prophets' answer is hard to hear. This came at the end of a long turning away, after warnings sent in compassion.
But that answer belongs to this event, not to every loss. Asked whose sin made a man blind, Jesus said, “Neither this man nor his parents sinned.”
Neither this man nor his parents sinned
At the center of Lamentations, one sufferer calls something to mind.
His mercies never fail. They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness!
That hope isn't a feeling. It's chosen in the dark, resting on who God is.
And the book still ends asking whether God has rejected them for good. Scripture keeps that unanswered prayer too.
God went with his people. He told Ezekiel he had been a sanctuary for them in the lands where they had gone.
In 539 BC Cyrus of Persia took Babylon and let the exiles go home. A new temple was finished in 516 or 515 BC.
And the prophets promised more than had been lost: a covenant written on the heart.
I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts.
Centuries later, Jesus wept over Jerusalem and foretold that it would be torn down again. That happened in AD 70.
In the temple courts he quoted Jeremiah's temple sermon. And he spoke of his own body as the temple, destroyed and raised in three days.
To this day the fast of Tisha B'Av remembers both temples.
As Jesus approached Jerusalem and saw the city, He wept over it
So why did God let it fall? The prophets say he did what he had warned, after long patience.
But the building was never what held him. He went with his people into exile, and he brought them home.
The temple fell. His mercies didn't.
Is the Bible true? Other films here go deep on the copies, the dates and the books.
This one asks something earlier: what would it mean for this book to be true?
Copying words correctly doesn't make them true. A lie can be preserved perfectly.
The Bible isn't one kind of writing. It holds histories, prayers, laws, prophets and letters.
Pause here and ask yourself: is a song true the same way a court record is?
Some Christians say Scripture is fully trustworthy in everything it sets out to teach. So ask what each part sets out to do.
Luke opens like a historian.
Having carefully investigated everything from the beginning, it seemed good also to me to write an orderly account for you
Most scholars now read the Gospels as ancient biographies. Richard Burridge's 1992 study, What Are the Gospels?, made that the consensus.
Ancient biographers arranged material by theme and summarized speeches as a matter of course.
But their center is a claim about what happened, one that could be proved false.
Some prayers argue with God.
How long, O LORD, must I call for help but You do not hear?
Job asks it chapter after chapter. Some psalms ask God to break the teeth of enemies.
Weigh this: what would it mean for a prayer like that to be true?
For many skeptics, the deepest problem isn't that the Bible's words were changed. It's that they weren't.
Laws that regulate slavery. Commands in Joshua to destroy whole towns.
That moves the question from, do we have the text, to, is the God of this text good? It's a better question, and it has pages of its own.
The Bible keeps sending prophets to people who already have the Scriptures. It expects its readers to get it wrong.
Paul's letters were read as Scripture very early. Yet one apostle admits another is hard to follow.
Some parts of his letters are hard to understand.
What does it claim about itself?
All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness.
And Jesus, resting an argument on one phrase of a psalm, said the Scripture cannot be broken.
Fair objection: isn't that a circle? It's true because it says so.
The first Christians couldn't have reasoned that way. They had no New Testament, only the Scriptures of Israel and the news that Jesus had been raised.
They trusted Him because they believed God had raised Him. Then they received the Scriptures the way He did.
He told experts in those Scriptures they'd missed what the book was for.
These are the very words that testify about Me, yet you refuse to come to Me to have life.
Christians who confess the Bible as God's word differ on how to say it.
Many evangelical churches confess it's without error. The Chicago Statement of 1978 says that isn't negated by “variant selections of material in parallel accounts, or the use of free citations.”
Others put the conviction differently. Faithful Christians still divide over which wording is right. This film doesn't choose.
There are honest limits. In Mark, Jesus places a story in the days of Abiathar the high priest. First Samuel names Ahimelech, Abiathar's father.
When the young Bart Ehrman argued around it, his professor, Cullen Story, wrote, “Maybe Mark just made a mistake.”
That verse still has no explanation everyone accepts. And no stone can show that a man rose from the dead.
Many young Christians absorb a faith in which the Bible stands or falls with winning every argument about every verse. We taught them that, usually without meaning to. The Bible never did.
So ask yourself: what would it take for you to trust an ancient book, any ancient book?
Then read one Gospel whole. Mark is the shortest. Notice what it keeps that anyone managing a reputation would have cut: Peter's denial.
John tells you why he wrote.
These are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in His name.
What happens when we die is one question. This film asks how the whole story ends.
Christian hope is specific: Christ's return, the dead raised in their bodies, the world judged in righteousness, and a renewed creation.
The creed of Constantinople, in 381, ends right there, looking for the resurrection of the dead, and the life of the world to come.
The Bible doesn't pretend death is nothing. Jesus wept at his friend's grave. And Paul calls death an enemy.
The last enemy to be destroyed is death.
So the final hope isn't a soul floating away. It's the body raised, as Jesus' body was.
In 1955, at Harvard, Oscar Cullmann argued that the New Testament hopes for resurrection, not the Greek idea of an immortal soul. Critics thought he overdrew it. He still changed the conversation.
Paul's picture is a seed. What is sown is perishable; it is raised imperishable.
Pause here and ask yourself. If bodies will be raised, does what we do with bodies now matter more than we thought?
The Bible's last pages don't show people leaving the earth for the sky. They show the holy city coming down out of heaven from God.
Around 180, Irenaeus argued that what passes away is the world's present form, not its substance. God doesn't say, I make new things. He says, Behold, I make all things new.
Christians differ on whether this creation will be renewed or replaced, and on whether its center is the renewed earth or seeing God's face. This film doesn't choose.
Then comes judgment. To us the word sounds like condemnation. In Scripture, to judge is to set things right: to stop the oppressor and rescue the oppressed.
After the wars in the former Yugoslavia, Miroslav Volf argued that only those who trust God to judge can lay down the sword of revenge.
Weigh it yourself. Would a world with no final judgment be kinder, or would it tell those who suffered most that it didn't matter?
He has set a day when He will judge the world with justice by the Man He has appointed.
But judgment raises the hardest question. What about hell?
In 1927 Bertrand Russell said, I do not myself feel that any person who is really profoundly humane can believe in everlasting punishment.
The argument is about proportion. A just punishment fits the wrong. Human wrongs are finite. Endless suffering isn't.
The Christian philosopher Marilyn McCord Adams asked the same in 1993. And grant what's true: the church has sometimes preached hell with relish, and used fear of it to control people.

Most of the church, with Augustine and the Reformation confessions, holds that the lost suffer conscious separation from God without end. C. S. Lewis wrote that the doors of hell are locked on the inside.
Others hold conditional immortality: God alone is immortal, and the finally impenitent at last perish. Edward Fudge argued it in 1982.
A smaller number, from Origen and Gregory of Nyssa to Thomas Talbott, hope God's love will restore all. Most of the church's confessions reject that hope.
Each answer carries a real difficulty. The first must face the proportion argument, and a suffering that heals no one.
The second must explain why Jesus set eternal punishment beside eternal life in one sentence. The third must face his warnings, which speak of no way back.
This film doesn't choose. Pause and ask yourself which difficulty seems heaviest, and why.
The strongest reply is Dostoevsky's Ivan Karamazov. I want to forgive. I want to embrace. I don't want more suffering.
The Christian answer begins by refusing one picture. Hell is not God's pleasure. Do I take any pleasure in the death of the wicked? declares the Lord GOD.
Judgment is borne by God before it falls on anyone. And no one knows who will be lost. Judgment belongs to Christ, who wept over Jerusalem.
The best thing about the new world isn't its river or its gates. It's that God lives there. The God who wept at a grave will wipe away every tear himself.
Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them.
The whole Bible keeps pointing back to one rescue. In Egypt, Abraham's family has become a nation of slaves, their lives bitter with hard labor in brick and mortar.
So God heard their groaning, and He remembered His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
From a bush that burns and isn't burned up, God sends a reluctant shepherd, Moses, to Pharaoh. Pharaoh answers with a question: who is the LORD, that I should obey him?
Ten plagues reply, judgment, Exodus says, against all the gods of Egypt. The last is the death of the firstborn.
Who is the LORD that I should obey His voice and let Israel go?
Each household marks its doorframe with a lamb's blood. Israel isn't spared because its people are better. A lamb dies in their place.
When I see the blood, I will pass over you.
It was a night of great sadness in Egypt, and Jewish tradition remembers it with gratitude and with grief.
A child at the table asks, “What does this service mean to you?” Pause and ask it yourself. Why begin a year of worship with one night?
Pharaoh changes his mind and pursues with his chariots. Trapped between an army and the water, the people panic. Moses says,
The LORD will fight for you; you need only to be still.
All night a strong east wind drives back the sea, and people who couldn't save themselves walk through on dry ground.
On the far shore Miriam leads the women with tambourines and dancing.
The LORD is my strength and my song, and He has become my salvation.
Many scholars argue from its language that this song is among the oldest poems in the Hebrew Bible. Others date it later.
The hard question: no Egyptian text mentions Israel's slavery, the plagues, or the departure.

Its most influential statement is The Bible Unearthed, by Israel Finkelstein and Neil Asher Silberman, in 2001. Exodus counts about 600,000 men on foot, besides women and children. That's two million or more, larger than all of Canaan then.
Forty years of wandering should leave pottery, hearths, graves. Sinai has yielded nothing that fits. So, they argued, the exodus is best read as a later national epic.
about 600,000 men on foot, besides women and children

Much of that is true. Nothing from Egypt or Sinai confirms the story directly, and the numbers are a real difficulty. Christians made it worse with claims like chariot wheels on the sea floor, which don't survive scrutiny.
Weigh this before the answer: would Egypt's monuments keep the memory of Egypt's humiliation?
The Egyptologist James Hoffmeier argued in 1997 that Egypt's royal records rarely record defeats, and herders in tents leave little to find.

What survives fits the setting: Semitic peoples in the eastern Nile Delta, a royal city named Rameses, Egyptian names like Moses and Phinehas. About 1208 BC, Pharaoh Merneptah's inscription already names Israel as a people in Canaan.
The date is argued. Counting back from First Kings 6:1 gives about 1446 BC. Others point to the name Rameses and place it in the thirteenth century.

The numbers are argued too. Some take them as written. Others note that elef, the Hebrew word for thousand, can also mean a clan, which makes the company far smaller. Some think a smaller group's escape became the whole people's story. This film doesn't choose.
Critics reply that peoples invent humble origins. Livy says crowds fled to Romulus's new city, free and slave alike.
Defenders answer that Rome's humble start is a detail. Israel's slavery is the center of its life. Its law begins,
I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.
Archaeology can't prove the exodus, and the date, the numbers, and the route are still open.
Christians read this rescue as the pattern of a greater one. At a Passover meal, Jesus called the cup the new covenant in his blood.
For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.
As God brought Israel out of slavery through death and water, so in Christ he brings his people out of sin and death. They receive that rescue. They don't earn it.
The Valley of Elah runs from the hills of Judah toward the Philistine plain, a natural road for an army pushing inland.
The Philistines stood on one hill and the Israelites stood on another, with the valley between them.
Israel's king is Saul, chosen to fight its battles, a head taller than his men. For forty days he doesn't move.
Morning and evening a champion comes out from Gath: Goliath. The Hebrew word for champion appears only in this chapter. It means the man of the between, who steps into the space between two armies.
Bronze helmet, armor of roughly 125 pounds, a spear shaft like a weaver's beam. One man for a whole people.
Saul and all the Israelites were dismayed and greatly afraid.

How tall? The standard Hebrew text says six cubits and a span, about nine and a half feet. The Dead Sea Scrolls copy of Samuel and the Greek translation say four cubits and a span. Still a giant in his day.
The oldest Greek manuscripts also lack whole stretches of this chapter, which suggests it circulated in more than one form.
He was six cubits and a span in height
David, the youngest of Jesse's eight sons, brings grain and bread to his brothers. Goliath shouts, the soldiers run, and David asks,
Just who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?
What the soldiers hear as a threat to Israel, David hears as an insult to the living God.
Pause here and ask yourself: two groups hear the same words. Why does one hear only danger, and the other hear God's name?
Saul says, you're just a boy. David answers with memory.
The LORD, who delivered me from the claws of the lion and the bear, will deliver me from the hand of this Philistine.
Faith here is memory put to work in a new danger. The king's armor doesn't fit. David takes it off and chooses five smooth stones. A sling wasn't a toy. Armies had trained slingers.
The center of the chapter is a speech, not a stone. Goliath curses David by his gods. David comes in the name of the LORD of Hosts, so the whole world will know there is a God in Israel.
It is not by sword or spear that the LORD saves; for the battle is the LORD’s.
David runs toward the battle line. One stone, and the champion falls facedown.
Thus David prevailed over the Philistine with a sling and a stone, without a sword in his hand.
Israel, frozen for forty days, charges. From here David's fame grows, and so does Saul's jealousy.
One old puzzle: in chapter 16 David already serves Saul as his harpist. Yet now Saul asks whose son he is.

Some say Saul, tormented, didn't recognize him. Others note a royal marriage was promised to the winner's family, so he's asking about the father. Many scholars think two accounts sit side by side. The text doesn't settle it.
Abner, whose son is this young man?
Weigh this before the answer: is this a story about believing in yourself, as if brave small people always beat big strong ones?
The chapter itself says the opposite. David isn't trusting himself. He trusts the God whose name Goliath insulted.
Readers still differ. Some draw from David a courage rooted in knowing whose battle it is. Others warn that First Samuel isn't a set of moral examples to copy.
Readers have long seen this pattern filled out in Christ, though the chapter is a battle story, not an allegory.
David fights for a people too afraid to fight, and his victory becomes theirs. Most readers are not David here. They're the soldiers on the hillside, delivered by another.
Jesus came to free those who all their lives were held in slavery by their fear of death.
So ask where you'd stand on that hill, and who went down into the valley for you.
From about 1980, Rollen Stewart held up John 3:16 signs at televised sporting events. The reference became one of the best known in the English-speaking world.
But the verse belongs to a conversation.
Nicodemus was a Pharisee, most likely a member of the Sanhedrin, the council in Jerusalem. Jesus calls him Israel's teacher.
He comes at night. Maybe to stay unseen. Maybe night was the hour for serious study.
John means you to notice: this man comes out of the dark toward the Light.
Rabbi, we know that You are a teacher who has come from God.
Jesus answers with a need: no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again.
The Greek word means again, or from above. Nicodemus hears a second time. Most commentators hear at least from above: a birth whose source is God.
The verb is passive. Nobody gives birth to himself. Ezekiel had promised a new heart and God's own Spirit. What startled was that Israel's own teacher needed it.
One Greek word means wind, breath and spirit. The wind blows where it wishes. You hear it. You can't steer it.
Pause here. What are you counting on: family, effort, standing? Jesus asked a new birth of the most religious man in the room.
The wind blows where it wishes. You hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it is going.
Then Jesus reaches for Numbers 21. The people spoke against God and Moses. Venomous snakes came, and many died.
They confessed, and the Lord told Moses, Make a fiery serpent and mount it on a pole. When anyone who is bitten looks at it, he will live.
Jewish readers insisted the metal didn't heal. The Mishnah says Israel was healed when they looked upward and set their hearts on their Father in heaven.
Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, that everyone who believes in Him may have eternal life.
To a first-century ear, lifted up on a pole meant crucifixion, in public view. Yet the same word means exalted.
Weigh a fair question. Why a look, and not a cure you could work for? Because faith here isn't an achievement. It's turning toward what God has provided.
For God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son, that everyone who believes in Him shall not perish but have eternal life.
Look at the small word so. It most naturally means in this way, not only so much. In 1999 Robert Gundry and Russell Howell argued that it points back to the lifting up.
The word shows the love's shape: a Son given and lifted up. His love is why there is a cross.
And the world? In John it usually means humanity turned away from God, the world that did not recognize him.
So the wonder isn't the world's size. It's the world's hostility.
Pause here. Which is harder to believe: that God loves the world, or that he loves you in particular.
the world did not recognize Him.
In John, to believe is to trust yourself to a person more than to agree with a statement. And eternal life is the life of the age to come, received now.
Christians differ on what world and everyone imply. Arminian readers say God's saving intention reaches every person.
Reformed readers, like John Owen in 1648, say God's love for the world issues in a special saving purpose for the elect, while the offer to all remains sincere. This film takes no side.
For God did not send His Son into the world to condemn the world, but to save the world through Him.
Yet there is a verdict. The Light has come into the world, but men loved the darkness rather than the Light. Loved is the same verb as verse 16.
Why prefer the dark? The reason is moral, not intellectual. We fear exposure.
John never says how Nicodemus answered.
Later he asks the council to give Jesus a fair hearing. And after the cross he brings about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes to bury him.
The man who came at night steps into the open. His faith came slowly, and John follows him with sympathy.
Nicodemus, who had previously come to Jesus at night

films.title: Psalm 23: the LORD is my shepherd

lines.text: Psalm 23 is the best-known psalm in the Bible. Read it slowly, one picture at a time.
The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.

In the ancient Near East, kings called themselves shepherds. Hammurabi of Babylon, in the eighteenth century BC, does it in the prologue to his laws. And God charged David to shepherd his people Israel.
Psalm 23 turns that around. The king is the sheep.
The heading says, A Psalm of David. Traditional readers note that David kept sheep before he was king. Many modern scholars read the heading as marking a collection, not an author.
No event is named, and it's been prayed in every generation because it isn't tied to one.
A Psalm of David.
Shepherding in Judah was hard, dangerous work in dry country. Green grass and quiet water had to be found, sometimes far away.
He makes me lie down in green pastures; He leads me beside quiet waters.
Sheep won't lie down unless they're fed and unafraid. Pause and ask yourself what you want most, and what it would take for you to rest.
He restores my soul; He guides me in the paths of righteousness for the sake of His name.
Paths of righteousness can mean right paths: tracks that lead where they should, not dead ends.
And notice why: for his name's sake. He's faithful to his own name.
Then the path drops into a ravine. The Hebrew word, traditionally the shadow of death, may simply mean deep darkness, where danger hides.
Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for You are with me.
Listen to the grammar turn. Until now the psalmist has spoken about God. At the darkest point, near the center of the poem, he speaks to him.
If you've come to this psalm carrying grief, notice what it doesn't promise. It doesn't promise a road around the valley. It promises company in it.
Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me.
The rod was a club for driving off predators, the staff a longer stick for guiding and rescuing.
Comfort here isn't softness. It's someone armed and attentive, standing between the flock and whatever hunts it.
Now the picture shifts from shepherd to host.
You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies.
A host who took a guest into his tent was bound to protect him, even from pursuers. So this is a fugitive welcomed as an honored guest while his enemies watch, unable to act.
Weigh this: the table is spread while the enemies are still there. Is that a smaller comfort, or a deeper one?
You anoint my head with oil; my cup overflows.
Oil on a guest's head meant welcome and honor. A cup that runs over meant lavish generosity. The guest gets more than safety.
Surely goodness and mercy will follow me all the days of my life,
Mercy here is chesed: loving devotion, the loyal love God has pledged to his people, love that holds when they have no claim on it.
And follow can mean pursue. Enemies hunted him. Now goodness and loving devotion pursue him, all his days.
and I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever.
The Hebrew, as traditionally read, says I will return. The ancient Greek says dwell, spelled almost the same. Either way, the psalm ends at home in God's presence.
The psalm that began in a field ends in a house.
The prophets promised that God himself would shepherd his scattered people, and set over them one shepherd from David's line. Centuries later, Jesus said,
I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep.
Good means the shepherd as a shepherd ought to be. A hired hand runs from the wolf. This shepherd lays down his life, in order to take it up again.
The New Testament never quotes Psalm 23 directly. But it adds this: the shepherd who walks with his sheep through the dark valley went into death for them.

films.title: Romans 8:28: what it promises, and what it does not

lines.text: Someone gets a hard diagnosis, or loses a person they love. And a friend, meaning well, says: everything happens for a reason.
And we know that God works all things together for the good of those who love Him, who are called according to His purpose.
Few verses are quoted more often to people in pain, and few are quoted more carelessly.
Take the slogan seriously. It reaches for something Christians believe and call providence.
God keeps the world in being. He works in and through everything that happens in it, and he directs it toward the ends he has purposed.

But the slogan turns it into a code to crack, as if every loss came with a readable reason. Jesus refused that. Asked about eighteen people killed when a tower fell at Siloam, he denied they were worse sinners.
Pause here and ask yourself. Does the verse say that everything is good? Read it again before you answer.
It doesn't. In our translation the subject is God. Some early manuscripts write the word God in; others don't. Either way, the sense is God's active purpose.
That is both more modest and more solid than the slogan.
What does all things cover? In this chapter: present sufferings, a creation in bondage to decay, and the list in verse 35.
Much of that list came from Paul's own life. He'd been beaten, shipwrecked and jailed.
He never calls those things good. He says they cannot defeat God's purpose.
Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall trouble or distress or persecution or famine or nakedness or danger or sword?
The verses just before are full of groaning. Creation groans. Believers groan. And the Spirit himself intercedes with groans too deep for words.
Paul doesn't treat groaning as a failure of faith. The Spirit helps us in our weakness, he says, and the word for helps means taking hold of a burden together with someone.
Verse 26 says what we don't know: how to pray. Verse 28 says what we do know. The promise was written from inside grief.
So what is the good? Paul leaves it open for one sentence, then defines it.
To be conformed to the image of His Son.
Not comfort. Not success. The good is becoming like Jesus, and nothing can defeat that purpose.
The Bible's classic picture of this is Joseph, sold by his own brothers.
Years later he tells them: what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good.
The same Hebrew verb, chashav, is used of the brothers and of God. One event, two intentions. The brothers are guilty of theirs. Joseph neither excuses them nor pretends the evil was good.
Here's a fair question to weigh. If God works in all things, how does that fit with real human choices?

Reformed readers, from Calvin on, say God ordains all that happens, through real human causes. Arminians, from Arminius and Wesley on, say he permits much he doesn't cause. Molinists, after Luis de Molina, point to what God knows free creatures would do.
They read foreknew in verse 29 differently too, yet agree its goal is likeness to Christ. And Reformed, Lutheran, Catholic and Wesleyan traditions alike deny that God is the author of sin.
And it doesn't promise that the illness will lift, or that the loss will be explained.
The verse does not promise that all things are good, only that God is working in all of them. Joseph understood his story only years later. Job never learned of the scene in heaven.
Pause here and ask yourself. Has this verse ever been quoted to you too quickly? What would it have sounded like with the whole chapter read to you?
Because the chapter ends with what the promise rests on. He who did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all.
In all these things, Paul says, not by escaping them, believers are more than conquerors. The victory is inside suffering, not after it.
And nothing in all creation will be able to separate them from the love of God in Christ Jesus. The chapter that opened with no condemnation ends with no separation.
nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

films.title: The Holy Spirit through the Bible

lines.text: Before light, land or life, the Bible's second verse already names him.
And the Spirit of God was hovering over the surface of the waters.
The Hebrew word is ruach. It can mean wind, breath, or spirit, and context decides which.
Some Bibles read “a wind from God.” But this verb for hovering is used elsewhere only of an eagle over its young: which favors a living presence over a gust.
That one word ties the Spirit to life itself. Job says,
The Spirit of God has made me, and the breath of the Almighty gives me life.
Pause here and ask yourself: whose breath are you breathing right now?
Then the Spirit comes on particular people for particular work: Bezalel the craftsman, Gideon the judge. And when Samuel anoints David,
the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David from that day forward.
The prophets spoke as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit. But it was a few, for a season.
Moses said, “I wish that all the LORD’s people were prophets.” The prophets turn that wish into God's promise. Through Ezekiel God says,
I will remove your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh.
And, “I will put My Spirit within you.” Not on a few leaders, but within a people.
After Jerusalem fell, in 587 or 586 BC, the exiles said, our bones are dried up, and our hope has perished.
God sets Ezekiel in a valley of very dry bones and asks, “Son of man, can these bones come to life?” What would you say?
Ezekiel answers, “only You know.” The bones come together, but there's no breath in them. Then he prophesies to the breath, and they stand up alive. It's Genesis 2 again: first a body, then breath.
Most scholars read it as the nation's return from exile. Many Christians also hear the resurrection in it. Both agree only God's word and Spirit give life to the dead.
Joel widens the promise past every line Israel drew.
I will pour out My Spirit on all people. Your sons and daughters will prophesy.
Servants too, without regard to age, sex, or social standing.
As Jesus comes up out of the Jordan, the heavens break open, the Spirit descends like a dove, and a voice says,
You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased.
Father, Son and Spirit, in one scene. Christians confess one God in three persons: one what, three whos. That's a mystery, something we can't see to the bottom of. It isn't a contradiction.
The night before he died, Jesus promised “another Advocate to be with you forever,” one called alongside to help.
A fair question: is the Spirit someone, or something? Jesus says “Him.” The Spirit teaches, can be grieved, and intercedes.
Lying to the Holy Spirit, Peter said, is lying to God. The Spirit isn't a force. He is God, as much a person as the Father and the Son.
Fifty days after Passover, at Pentecost, Jerusalem is full of pilgrims. Suddenly a sound like a mighty rushing wind came from heaven and filled the whole house.
Tongues like flames of fire rest on each of them, and the crowd hears the wonders of God in its own languages.
Peter says, “this is what was spoken by the prophet Joel.” Then the gift crosses boundaries, to Samaritans, then to Gentiles.
Is Pentecost a pattern for every believer, or a once-for-all event?

Pentecostal and many charismatic Christians see a baptism in the Spirit that may follow conversion. Many evangelicals say every believer receives the Spirit at conversion. Some hold that the miraculous gifts continue, others that they ceased with the apostles. This film doesn't choose.
All confess that the Spirit lives in everyone who belongs to Christ. Together they are God's temple.
Do you not know that you yourselves are God’s temple, and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?
On the Bible's last page the Spirit is still speaking, with the bride, all God's people.
The Spirit and the bride say, “Come!”
The Spirit who hovered over the first waters now offers the water of life, freely, to anyone who is thirsty.
